question:
Toronto Hydro proposes a Demand-Related Variance Account (“DRVA”) with two subaccounts (p.
36). An Expenditure Variances subaccount
“would record the symmetrical revenue requirement impacts, including PILs, arising from the
variance between 2025-2029 planned and actual expenditures related to the following capital and
operations programs: Customer Connections, Customer Operations, Stations Expansion, Load
Demand, Non-Wires Solutions, Generation Protection Monitoring and Control and Externally-
Initiated Plant Relocations and Expansions (collectively the “Demand-Related Investments”).”
Toronto Hydro states on p. 41 that
“In circumstances where demand-related investments are lower than planned, the subaccount
would protect ratepayers by ensuring that (i) they do not pay for demand-driven work that can be
deferred, and (ii) funds are not repurposed to manage variances in other aspects of the plan that
are not driven by demand.”

a) Please provide analysis which demonstrates that the use of a variance account best serves
customers from a cost perspective, including, but not limited to, the aggressive use of load
management and other techniques to efficiently accommodate demand growth and other
changes in system use.
b) Why is it necessary to track the entirety of these various costs when
ix) a sizable share of these costs will result from normal demand growth;
x) a customer growth escalator can address many/most costs of customer connections and
customer operations with minimal regulatory cost or diminution of cost-containment
incentives;
xi) variance account treatment is less controversial and likely to be approved for costs of
NWAs, beneficial electrification, generation protection monitoring and control, Getting
Ontario Connected Act compliance, and externally-initiated plant relocations and
expansions.
response:
In circumstances where demand-related investments can be adjusted down based on updated
forecasting inputs, the subaccount would protect ratepayers by ensuring that (i) they do not pay for
demand-driven work that can be deferred, and (ii) funds are not repurposed to offset variances in
other aspects of the plan that are not driven by demand. Such circumstances can occur due to a
number of factors, including the impact of greater use of load management techniques, material
changes in economic conditions that slow down the pace of growth in forecasted demand, or market
constraints that alter the adoption of electrified technologies such as EVs. For more information
about the use of “use of load management techniques” please see Toronto Hydro’s response to
interrgoatory 1B-Staff-40.

Please refer to Exhibit 1B, Tab 2, Schedule 1 at pages 37 to 46 for detailed evidence of the need and
justification for the Expenditure Variance Subaccount.
Implicit in this question is an assumption that what was “normal load growth” in the past will
continue in the future. It is evident that the future will not be like the past in terms of load and
demand. For example, and as noted in the above-referenced evidence at pages 38-39, Toronto
Hydro saw a significant increase in the volume and complexity of load connections in the current rate
period. From 2020 to 2022, high voltage connections (which often require system expansion work)
increased by 27.6 percent, with a substantial increase in larger commercial and multi-use projects
requiring greater than 10 MVA of demand load per project, as well data centers with larger loads
(e.g., 30-50 MVA) than ever before. These circumstances resulted in gross expenditures in the
Customer Connections program that are expected to be approximately 1.75 times greater than the
forecast that formed the basis of 2020-2024 rates. As a result, capital in-service additions related to
demand-driven investments in System Access were approximately $153 million (32.5 percent)
greater than the amounts included in base rates in the current period.
A “customer growth escalator” does not address the business concern underlying the proposed
DRVA. As noted in the above-referenced evidence at page 35, due to a confluence of external factors
(i.e., policy, technology and consumer behaviour changes) Toronto Hydro is entering a period of
unprecedented change and transformation, as customers, communities and governments at all
levels are actively embarking on an energy transition to mitigate the existential and economic
impacts of climate change. Decarbonization is expected to create new roles for electricity, including
as an energy source for transportation and building heating systems. While there is certainty that
fundamental change is ahead, there are degrees of uncertainty about how that change will unfold
(e.g., the pace and adoption of electrified technologies such as EVs and heat pumps; the role of low-
emission gas; and the scale of local vs. bulk electricity supply). A “customer growth escalator” would
fail to address the noted concerns with respect to uncertainty and variability in demand, and would
not provide Toronto Hydro the necessary flexibility to manage demand-driven aspects of its plan in
order to protect both rate payers and the utility from structural unknowns in forecasted costs and
revenues.
Toronto Hydro believes that many of the same considerations which render the listed
programs/priorities more likely to be approved for variance account treatment, apply to the other
programs that form part of the DRVA Expenditure Account proposal, as detailed in Exhibit 1B, Tab 2,
Schedule 1 at pages 37 to 46:
•
Customer Connections and Customer Operations: Investments in these programs are driven
by the utility’s fundamental obligation to serve customers who want to connect to the
system. In addition to enabling beneficial electrification, the need for investment is also
driven by other important policy considerations, including governments’ priorities to
accelerate transit and housing development.1
•
Stations Expansions and Load Demand: Investments in these programs are subject to an
ongoing regional planning process. Outputs of that process, which may extend beyond the
timelines for adjudicating this application, or additional updates to regional plans that may
be necessary during the 2025-29 rate term, could modify planned investments under the
Stations Expansion and Load Demand programs. For example, Station Expansion projects
such as Scarborough TS and Load Demand investments in the Horseshoe area of the grid,
which were deferred through the evidence updated filed on January 29, 2024 may have to
be pulled forward if needs in these areas of the grid exceed current expectations due to
either (or both) normal demand growth and beneficial electrification.
1 https://news.ontario.ca/en/backgrounder/1002525/more-homes-built-faster-act-2022

Similar to the above, Toronto Hydro submits the achievement of a state of grid modernization

Yes, the quantitative basis for selecting a 99% target is Toronto Hydro’s 2014-2022 average

question:
On pages 2, 7, and 43 of Reference 1, Toronto Hydro has proposed a stretch or efficiency factor of
0.15%, valued at $16.4 million over the term. Achieving the stretch factor is forecast to represent a
sustained savings of $6.9M per year by 2029. Toronto Hydro has assigned a performance incentive
to the achievement of these forecast efficiency achievements, valued at 15% of the $65M total PIM
performance factor.

a) Please confirm the value of the PIM attached to efficiency savings, which appears to be
$9.75M (15% of $65M).
b) Please recalculate the value of the stretch factor net of the achievement of the PIMs, or
confirm that it is 0.09% ((9.75/16.4)*(0.15)). Please show all calculations.
c) Please explain the rationale for this stretch factor design and net value, including its
interaction within the PIMs framework, and with reference to the OEB’s standard stretch
factor values.
response:
The total proposed incentive is $65 million based on performance against a balanced scorecard.
15% of scorecard achievement is assigned to Efficiency Achievements. 15% of $65 million is $9.75
million.

The empirically-derived stretch factor of 0.15% proposed for the 2025 to 2029 rate term is not, and
will not be net of any PIM achievement. Customers will directly receive the benefits of reduced rates
through the 2025 to 2029 term as a result of the 0.15% stretch factor, which will not be adjusted for
any PIM achievement. The purpose of the Efficiency Achievement metric, as articulated on page 42
of Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, is “holding the utility accountable for delivering sustained (and
quantifiable) efficiency benefits to customers in the next rebasing application.”
The purpose of the Efficiency Achievement metric is to improve the incentive signals which are
otherwise naturally embedded in incentive regulation; specifically, near-term cost control. One
potential route to financial incentives under standard incentive regulation is the pursuit of short-
duration cost cutting, or the deferral of important capital work which will ultimately result in back-
logged and increased spending in subsequent years. The Efficiency Achievement metric requires that
the utility demonstrate the achievement of sustained savings which would persist into subsequent
rate terms. Please see 1B-SEC-20 (f) for more information.

question:

Please explain the basis for the assumption that “5 years of LDR is sufficient to avoid the capital
investment,” citing examples or direct experience if available.
response:
The assumption of 5 years is based on experience and engineering planner judgement. As noted in
Exhibit 2B Section E.7 on pages 10-12, Toronto Hydro has been successful in avoiding incremental
load transfers in the Manby TS and Horner TS service areas through the application of targeted
demand response. This has allowed Toronto Hydro to reassess the need for these load transfers
each year and make the decision to defer them. By the end of the five-year rate-period, the load
transfers were no longer necessary. The assumption of five years is subject to change based on the
specific area targeted and was selected for the purpose of planning based on the best available
assumptions and information at this time.

question:
Clearspring’s power distributor cost model has three scale variables: the number of customers
served, a peak load variable, and area. This model also includes second-order (quadratic and
translog) terms for these variables. This treatment adds six scale-related variables to the model for
a total of nine and results in custom cost elasticities with respect to scale variables for Toronto
Hydro.
An ongoing discussion in Ontario Custom IR proceedings is whether a rolling average of past peak
demands or a ratcheted peak demand variable are better for a power distributor cost model.
An important result of cost theory is that cost should rise monotonically with output.

a) What are the estimated custom cost elasticities with respect to these three scale variables
for Toronto Hydro?
b) Parameter estimates for output variables may be assessed for consistency with the
monotonicity condition predicted by cost theory. Reference 2 is an example of such a study
in a report to the Australian Energy Regulator. Are Clearspring’s scale variable parameter
estimates in each year of the sample consistent with the monotonicity conditions predicted
by cost theory? Do any other sampled companies have violations?
c) The peak load variable that Clearspring uses in its model is a rolling average of past peak
load values. Up to ten past values are averaged to the extent that data are available. If the
sample period were shortened by ten years, wouldn’t this permit ten-year averages for all
years? If ratcheted peak demand was then calculated the same way for Toronto Hydro as
for the sampled US distributors, why would a moving average peak demand variable be
better than a ratcheted peak demand variable?
d) Did Clearspring try ratcheted peak demand as an alternative to the rolling average? If so,
which had stronger statistical support?
e) Does the company believe that the number of customers it reports on the RRR is
significantly affected by high rise housing where the building is only counted as one
“customer”? If so, please provide a rough estimate of the number of unmetered
residential customers (1 dwelling = 1 customer) that are jointly served from a single meter.
Is serving one customer with 100 tenants more costly than serving 100 separately-metered
and separately sited households? If so, why?
f) Did Clearspring consider using other normalization factors other than number of customers
due to the stated concern regarding the quantity of high-rise building? What other
normalization factors were considered but rejected? If no other normalization factors
were considered, why not in consideration of Toronto Hydro concerns regarding using
customer count?
response:
We calculated the first derivative with respect to each output to calculate the custom elasticities.
The equation for the custom customer elasticity that we calculated is, thus, the first order
customer coefficient plus the coefficient on the quadratic customer variable times the natural log
of the mean-scaled customer value plus the coefficient on interaction with customers and peak
demand multiplied by the natural log of the mean-scaled peak demand variable plus the coefficient
on the interaction with the customers and service area variable multiplied by the natural log of the
mean-scaled service area variable. For the custom peak demand elasticity and the area elasticity
we conducted the same calculation procedure but using the peak demand and area first order,
quadratic, and interaction terms.
Since the custom elasticities do not change in any way that would be material to this analysis from
year to year for the same utility, the 2021 values for Toronto Hydro are calculated to be 0.235 for
customers, 0.895 for peak demand, and -0.062 for service area.

Given the flexibility of the translog cost function it leaves open the possibility of specific output
variable elasticities being negative as the model adjusts for economies of scale and interactions
with other output variables. In the case of Toronto Hydro it is the service area custom elasticity
that is negative. This means that the cost benchmark for Toronto Hydro would decline in the model
if Toronto Hydro somehow added service territory area to its service territory variable value. Yet, in
the real world, it is difficult to imagine how this would occur and Toronto Hydro at the same time
not adding customers and peak demands. The additions of the customers and peak demands
would raise Toronto Hydro’s benchmark costs likely more than the service area variable would
reduce it. There are other instances of custom output elasticities being negative within the sample.
The majority of them are regarding the service area variable, similar to Toronto Hydro.

To accommodate all ten years within the ten-year sample average, Toronto Hydro’s first year must
be 2011 since its first year of peak demand data is 2002. The sample has peak demand data
collected from 1994, indicating that 2003 could be the first year where a rolling average variable
would have ten years available to calculate it.
Clearspring’s sample begins in 2000 which matches the start year that we used in the last
distribution total cost benchmarking research for Hydro One in EB-2021-0110. In Clearspring’s
report in that proceeding we explained the rationale for using an average peak demand variable
rather than a ratcheted one. One reason includes Clearspring considering the merits of and then
responding to intervenors who in the past questioned how it makes sense that a ratcheted peak
demand variable can never decrease even after years of falling peak demands. The total cost
research is focused on the long-run total costs of utilities. This is why capital costs are included into
the analysis and Clearspring goes back to the 1940’s to gather cost data and determine those costs.
To say that utilities will never adjust costs downward to declining peak demands is not accurate
and so the peak demand variable should be able to decline if that is the reality of the situation.
Clearspring agrees there will be a lag and a residual cost impact to prior high peak demand values
which is why we used the 10-year rolling average approach. The second rationale for the rolling
average peak demand variable versus the ratcheted approach is that a lot of the focus on the
benchmarking research results in this context are on the projected years of 2025 to 2029. Those
peak demands are weather normalized expectations, or averages, around the probabilities of
extreme or mild weather outcomes. Since the peak demand forecasts themselves are essentially
averages, using a variable that is itself an average is the more consistent approach in Clearspring’s
view.

Yes, Clearspring did calculate the variable. The first order ratcheted peak demand variable while
still highly statistically significant is less so than the 10-year rolling peak demand used by
Clearspring. The t-stat on the ratcheted peak demand is 13.82 versus a t-stat of 22.16 for the rolling
average variable. This indicates that it is the rolling average variable that has the stronger t-
statistic.

As discussed in lines 18-23 on page 11 of Exhibit 4, Tab 1, Schedule 1, Toronto Hydro serves far
more electricity users through bulk-metering and competitive sub-metering arrangements than its
actual customer count indicates and the utility estimates that it serves at least 340,000 end-
consumers behind bulk meters.
Serving 100 separately metered and sited households (e.g. in a multi-unit residential building suite
metered by Toronto Hydro), typically drives some additional billing, payment processing and
customer contact costs due to the greater number of account holders, compared to a single bulk
metered customer with 100 tenants/occupants behind the meter. Other than these costs related to
account transactions, there is no material OM&A cost difference between the two types of
customers.

We did identify this challenge as a possible candidate for a business condition variable or other
possible correction, however, no feasible normalization factors surfaced because of the lack of data
visibility into the sampled utilities regarding this condition. Not including a normalization factor
that adjusts for this cost challenge likely disadvantages Toronto Hydro in the benchmarking
research.

SUPPLEMENTAL RESPONSE – PREPARED BY TORONTO HYDRO:
Regarding the Updated Investment Plan tables provided above, please see Toronto Hydro’s
response to 2B-SEC-42, part (c).
Regarding the IRM Scenario tables provided above, Toronto Hydro notes that a substantial
deterioration in unplanned outages under the IRM scenario is offset by a material improvement in
Scheduled Outages in the projection methodology. This large swing results from the application of
Toronto Hydro’s limited approach to projecting Scheduled Outages. As discussed in Exhibit 2B,
Section E2, pages 16-19, Toronto Hydro’s recent and ongoing implementation of more advanced
network management and utility analytics capabilities has led to the capture of more detailed and
accurate outage information, with the most significant impacts being on the Scheduled Outage
cause code. These impacts began in 2022, and for this reason, Toronto Hydro is not able to rely on
a multi-year statistical approach to forecast Scheduled Outages. The best-efforts approach that
Toronto Hydro applied in order to provide a Scheduled Outages projection for Clearspring’s
benchmarking study was to take the actual SAIDI and SAIFI impacts from Scheduled Outages in
2022, and relate those impacts to the dollars invested in the subset of programs that
overwhelmingly drive Scheduled Outages. The utility then applied this simple ratio to the
magnitude of future planned spending. In reality, the utility expects that the ratio of Scheduled
Outage impacts to spending will vary materially from year-to-year depending on the mix of project
work executed. The application of such a limited and linear approach for Scheduled Outages to an
expenditure reduction of the magnitude contemplated in the IRM scenario is of limited value. A
reduction in spending of this magnitude would result in a fundamentally different operational
reality than the one captured by Toronto Hydro’s historical reliability performance.

Provide detailed explanation of increase in Billing O&M cost from 2018 to 2022 of more than
double 2018 customer billing costs.
Explain how productivity and economies of scale was not achieved with the adjustment of billing
period?
response:
The Billing O&M costs provided in Table 10 do not provide a consistent representation of Toronto
Hydro’s unit cost per customer over the 2018-2022 period. The key contributing factors are: 1) the
introduction of monthly billing costs into the calculation; and 2) enhanced mapping precision
between the Ontario Energy Board USoA accounts 5315 and 5320 following the utility’s conversion
from the its legacy accounting system, Ellipse, to its current accounting system, SAP, in 2019.
As shown in Table 1, when USoA accounts 5315 and 5320 are combined from 2018 to 2022,
Toronto Hydro’s costs are accurately represented, including the impact of monthly billing starting
in 2020. Other variances are explained throughout Exhibit 4, Tab 2, Schedule 14.

As shown above, costs are relatively flat during the period of 2018 to 2022, when normalized for the
inclusion of $4.8 million in incremental costs for the conversion from bi-monthly billing to monthly
billing in 2020. A detailed discussion of the impact on costs related to the mandatory transition to
monthly billing can be found in Toronto Hydro’s 2020-2024 CIR rate application.1
The vast majority of costs associated with billing customers monthly are not subject to economies
of scale benefits. For example, postage, paper and printing, and payment processing costs, which
combined make up 64% of the incremental operational costs, are directly related to the number of
bills sent.
To minimize the incremental labour costs, Toronto Hydro undertook a number of initiatives,
including automation, process improvements, outsourcing and campaigns to drive ebill adoption.
An example was the replacement of "gatekeeper systems" which gather and transmit data from
meters to Toronto Hydro's billing system, which resulted in more timely and accurate data being
gathered automatically and reduced the labour (and associated costs) required to manually collect
and estimate hard to read meters. Along with the higher transactional volumes, labour economies
of scale were further improved through these initiatives, such that the FTE per 100,000 bills issued

question:
The material challenges outlined in section 3, along with customer feedback and the principle of
least regrets investments established investment priorities for Toronto Hydro’s capital plan.
Specifically, Toronto Hydro notes the importance of investments including Distributed Energy
Resources to support “Growth & City Electrification”.
Question (A):
a) Does Toronto Hydro evaluate proposed DERs to determine if they will increase or decrease
system reliability during summer peak demand, winter peak demand, or during peak
generation periods of the proposed DER technology?
b) How does Toronto Hydro allocate the costs of system investments needed to mitigate any
negative reliability impacts that may be associated with implementation of specific DER
technologies in specific parts of its system?
c) Please identify the incremental investments in this application that are required to enable
Toronto Hydro to integrate new energy storage batteries into its system.
i.
Please explain why such investments would be needed in the planning period.
Considering that energy storage batteries have been utilized by other utilities as a non-wires
alternative technology to help defer or eliminate the need for wires investments, please explain
why this would not also apply to Toronto Hydro.
response:
Yes. Toronto Hydro performs connection impact assessments (CIA) to assess the impact of
connecting DERs on the system and evaluates criteria required to be met to maintain the stability
of the grid including during peak demand periods. This assessment takes into consideration the
Minimum-Load-to-Generation Ratio, a key determinant of grid stability.

Please see Toronto Hydro’s response to 2B-Staff-160 part (c).

Please see 2B-Staff-250 for a response to Toronto Hydro’s ESS investments in 2025-2029 and an
explanation for why such investments are needed.

Please refer to Toronto Hydro’s responses to 1B-Staff-88 and 1B-Staff-89 for information about the
utility’s non-wires strategy, investments and proposed incentives. Toronto Hydro is agnostic to the
technology (type of DER) or approach (load curtailment) utilized by aggregators or customers to
deliver dispatchable demand response capacity. As such, participants relying on energy storage
batteries are welcome to offer capacity into Toronto Hydro’s Local Demand Response market, if
they are able to provide the required service. Please see the evidence in Exhibit 2B Section E7.2 for
more information about the Non-Wires Solutions program.

question:
In Reference 1, Toronto Hydro shows that Toronto Hydro’s customer count has been slowing and is
projected to average 0.3% annually in the last three years of the rate period. The same reference
shows a downward trend in normalized MVA that is forecast to continue.
In Reference 2, Toronto Hydro states that “Toronto Hydro distributes electricity to Canada’s largest
- and North America’s second fastest growing city.”
Reference 4 indicates the City of Toronto’s population growth rate will slow.

a) Please explain Toronto Hydro’s view of the importance of absolute increase in population
as compared to the growth rate of a population in the context of planning a distribution
system. Please confirm that in the context of Toronto Hydro’s distribution system planning,
absolute growth is a more important consideration than the rate of growth. If not, please
explain.
b) Please reconcile the apparent discrepancy between the statement that the City of
Toronto’s population is growing, in absolute terms, more than other cities with Toronto
Hydro’s forecasts showing slowing system load growth rates and the Ontario Ministry of
Finance’s projections that population growth is slowing for the City of Toronto.
response:
Reference 1 above relates to customer and load growth changes from 2018 to 2029 for the
purpose of establishing a customer and load growth forecast to determine revenue to be collected
through rates, as fully described in Exhibit 3.
Reference 2 above contextualizes the size and characteristics of Toronto Hydro’s system and
customer base. Similar information is relied upon in the productivity evidence at Exhibit 1B, Tab 3,
Schedule 3 at pages 2 to 4, wherein Toronto Hydro describes its unique characteristics as a dense
urban distributor and the resulting operational challenges that it must manage in connecting and
serving its customers and carrying out prudent and necessary work to keep the system safe and
reliable in accordance with good utility practice.
Neither of the above references relate to growth for the purposes of distribution system planning,
which is articulated in full in Exhibit 2B, and summarized in Section A of that Exhibit at page 10:
“The growth is concentrated in certain pockets, namely the downtown core and along the transit
corridors, and is oriented vertically with a continuing trend of high-rise developments. This has
resulted is a marked need for new housing, transit solutions, and infrastructure, all of which needs
to be serviced by Toronto Hydro in the years to come.”
As outlined throughout the evidence in Exhibit 2B, distribution system planning is complex and
relies on a long list of varied inputs and planning considerations. There is no single metric of growth
relied upon to inform system planning.

Based on the response in part (a) above, Toronto Hydro submits there is no discrepancy, as
absolute growth and growth rates are referenced for different purposes in different contexts.
Both Reference 3 and Reference 4 are based on Statistics Canada data released in January 2023.
Reference 3 looks at growth over the preceding 12-month period and concludes that Toronto’s
population grew by 138,240 people, which is second only to Dallas-Fort Worth-Arlington in the cities
compared. Reference 4, on the other hand, is prospective and looks at population projections from
2022-2046. Reference 4 notes that Toronto’s population is projected to rise from 3.03 million in 2022
to 4.20 million in 2046, which is the largest population gain among the census divisions, but that the
rate growth of 37.7 percent is slightly slower than the provincial rate of growth of 43.6 percent.

prevent deterioration from current service levels and investing “the minimum level
necessary.”
g) Please discuss the proposal to maintain outage frequency in the context of the OEB’s
statement in Reference 2 that “The [Renewed Regulatory Framework] is intended to
elevate utility performance by creating incentives for superior performance.”
response:
Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management Process (refer to Exhibit 2B, Section D) combined with the
necessary funding and resources to execute the work programs outlined in the 2025-2029
investment plan, and the performance incentives proposed in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1 will
enable the utility to attain the proposed System Reliability targets for Outage Duration and Outage
Frequency.

Yes. All of the above are part of the 2025-2029 investment plan and rate application.

Please refer to the response in part a.

Toronto Hydro cannot comment on a hypothetical future scenario the parameters of which are
unclear and speculative. The utility notes however that in its experience as a performance-drive
organization, the achievement of the targets can be attributed to a combination of operational
management, innovative approaches, adaptability, collaboration, and risk management. Effective
decision-making is at the crux of all these factors. In a balanced incentive regime, where performance
targets are set in a challenging but achievable way, the utility is encouraged to optimize decision-
making towards achieving performance objectives.
In a regulatory regime that focuses predominately on financial/cost outcomes, decisions are
optimized to manage profitability, efficiency and cost containment. Over time and/or under certain
circumstances (e.g., the utility faces new requirements or rising cost pressures) this may compromise
the utility’s ability to achieve target service quality performance objectives.
Toronto Hydro believes that both types of incentives are important to drive effective decision-
making and ensure that there is an appropriate balance of risk/reward in the regulatory framework.
That is why its proposed X-factor includes both an empirical-based efficiency factor and a
performance-focused incentive mechanism. For more information, please refer to the Rate
Framework evidence in Exhibit 1B, Tab 2, Schedule 1 at pages 29-33.

Please see response to (d) above.

Refer to response in part d).

effectiveness of the performance incentive regime. To apply this statement in a wholesale manner
to each and every performance objective would run contrary to other important considerations in

regulation that is based on the achievement of outcomes that ensure that Ontario’s electricity system

references:

question:
Toronto Hydro states the use of Local Demand Response (LDR) to avoid capital spent on load
transfers resulting in significant long-term savings for ratepayers.

a) Please provide the benefit-cost analysis, or equivalent document, that supports Toronto
Hydro’s selection of target stations for demand response and those which have not been
proposed, including: Fairbank TS, Finch TS, Bathurst TS, Manby TS, Leslie TS, Cecil TS,
Strachan TS, and Copeland TS.
b) Please list any other LDR projects that were considered but rejected for the 2025 to 2029
period.
response:
As noted on pages 8 and 9 of the updated (January 29th, 2024) Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2, the
Flexibility Services program will target Finch TS, Manby TS, Cecil TS, Strachan TS, Leslie TS and
Copeland TS. The program is not currently focused on Fairbank TS or Bathurst TS, but should the
opportunity and need arise to target these stations, Toronto Hydro will investigate the possibility of
doing so. A key feature of the Flexibility Services program is that it can easily adapt in terms of
scope and location to meet the most pressing system needs. The program target areas will shift
based on needs, as has been the case in previous LDR programs.
As noted in Toronto Hydro’s response to the OEB’s stakeholder consultation on the Benefit – Cost
Analysis Framework for Addressing Electricity System Needs (EB-2023-0125), submitted on
February 1, 2023, Toronto Hydro applies pre-screening criteria when selecting potential
applications of NWSs, and selects projects that can be clearly defined and linked to a system need.
These projects are then put through a cost-benefit analysis to ensure the application of NWSs is
cost-effective. For more information on the cost-benefit analysis that has been undertaken for the
selected stations, please see Interrogatory 1B-Staff-89.

As described in Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2, the Flexibility Services program (i.e. LDR) directly supports
Load Demand by identifying opportunities to defer or avoid bus-level load transfers when and
where it is appropriate. As noted in the evidence, all stations that are targeted for bus-level relief in
2025-2029 were evaluated and considered for the LDR program. Some of these stations are
excluded (i.e. Dufferin TS, Terauley TS, Esplanade TS, Horner TS and Windsor TS) as the planned
transfers are either carry-over projects that were deferred in 2020-2024, or projects where
overloading is not the primary driver. The work planned for these stations is described in Exhibit
2B, Section E5.3. All six of the remaining stations that are expected to require bus-level load
transfers in the 2025-2029 period (i.e. Finch TS, Manby TS, Cecil TS, Strachan TS, Leslie TS and
Copeland TS) will be targeted for LDR capacity.

references:
Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, Section 2.4.3, Pages 46-56
Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2.1
question:
Toronto Hydro provides details of its proposed system capacity (non-wires) proposals, including the
LDR and performance incentive structure. Toronto Hydro proposes a budget of $5.7 million to deploy
an expanded version of its LDR initiative to address system capacity constraints and procure 30 MW
of flexible system capacity to displace and defer the need for load transfers in the Horseshoe North
area over the 2025-2029 term.

a) Please discuss what considerations Toronto Hydro undertook about expanding the LDR
program greater than 30 MW, including cost, impact on neighboring stations, ability to
procure necessary capacity and any subsequent changes to performance incentive
structures.
b) Please discuss the rationale for limiting LDR capacity at 30 MW for the 2025 to 2029 period.
c) Please discuss what considerations are required if the LDR program was to be leveraged to
alleviate long-term capacity needs for the various stations identified.
d) Please discuss and provide any analysis undertaken to consider similar LDR initiatives in
other areas of Toronto Hydro’s system that have identified constraints, including Horseshoe
East and West. Please indicate why similar projects have not been proposed for additional
areas on the system.
e) Please discuss what considerations and analysis was conducted by Toronto Hydro related to
CDM programs being offered in its service territory, including those in partnership with other
entities, including the IESO and the Local Initiatives Program during the 2025-2029 period.
f) Please discuss the Benefit Stacking Pilot that is supported by the IESO Grid Innovation Fund
and OEB’s Innovation Sandbox, including project timelines and how Toronto Hydro expects
to apply findings from the pilot project.
response:
Toronto Hydro considered the following key factors in setting the 30 MW target:
Resource Availability: Toronto Hydro’s experience shows that procurement of targeted demand
response (“DR”) for the purpose of capital deferral/avoidance is most successful when targeting
areas with a higher penetration of large loads (e.g., 1 MW or more, or large groupings of 100 kW or
more customers), as these customer types are more likely to be able to curtail on demand. The utility
selects stations with a high penetration of these customer types when possible, and sets achievable
targets that reflect the anticipated availability of DR amongst these customers. During the 2020-2024
rate period, Toronto Hydro set a target of 10 MW for a group of two stations (Manby TS and Horner
TS), and even this modest target proved to be challenging from a procurement perspective (see
below for details). For a group of six stations, Toronto Hydro set an ambitious goal of 30 MW (10 MW
per 2 stations), which reflects both the utility’s experience and commitment to continuous
improvement with respect to non-wires solutions.
Market Dynamics: Local Demand Response (“LDR”) is subject to market forces that could impact the
outcome of the program. In the current Etobicoke Pilot, the utility intended to procure 10MW but
could only secure 4 MW for the first summer (2023). This a reflection of available market capacity,
particularly as many resources are already committed to other programs (e.g., IESO’s Capacity
Auction, the Industrial Conservation Initiative (“ICI”). Aggregators (i.e., participants in LDR) expressed
that significant time and effort is required to acquire capacity for new programs, and that the average
time required to onboard new capacity for a new program could be anywhere between 6 to 12
months, resulting is some participants choosing to stick with existing market obligations and forego
participation in new programs. These are important factors to consider when setting reasonable
targets for non-wires solutions (“NWS”).
Other Considerations: In setting the 30 MW target, Toronto Hydro also considered the cost recovery
impacts of acquiring DR capacity (please see Exhibit 2B Section E7.2 for details) in addition to many
other urgent and important operational requirements that the utility must address in the next rate
term as summarized in the OM&A Overview evidence at Exhibit 4, Tab 1, Schedule 1, and detailed
throughout the programmatic evidence in Exhibit 4, Tab 2. The utility also considered the ongoing
regulatory uncertainty with respect to performance incentives and cost recovery for investments
that are needed to develop capabilities in this emerging area of focus. Coupled with the operational
and market risks identified above, these considerations led Toronto Hydro to set a challenging but
achievable target of 30MW.

For DR to replace a permanent, long-term capacity investment, Toronto Hydro needs confidence that
this market-based product can deliver the same safety and reliability requirements as a tried and
tested conventional wires solution at a cost-effective price. At this time, adequate volumes of DR
resources are not available to meet these requirements. As noted in part (a), it can be difficult to
procure even 10 MW of DR. To avoid larger scale, long-term station investments, Toronto Hydro
would need to procure upwards of 50 MW in one station area. Furthermore, to rely on DR at this
scale, Toronto Hydro would need to pay a high $/MW-day daily capacity payment along with
potential energy payments, for each day that the resource is relied upon. As the market matures and
more resources become available, Toronto Hydro will evaluate the feasibility and cost-effectiveness
of using DR to replace longer-term capacity investments.

As described in Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2, the Flexibility Services program (i.e. LDR) directly supports
Load Demand by identifying opportunities to defer or avoid bus-level load transfers when and where
it is appropriate. As noted in the evidence, Toronto Hydro evaluated all the stations that are targeted
for capacity bus-level relief in 2025-2029, including those in Horseshoe East and West, as well as
Downtown.1 From this evaluation, the utility selected six stations that are expected to require bus-
level load transfers in the 2025-2029 period (i.e. Finch TS, Manby TS, Cecil TS, Strachan TS, Leslie TS
and Copeland TS) for LDR capacity. The target areas could shift based on system needs, similar to
previous LDR programs, because as noted in Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2 on pages 8-9, the ability to easily
adapt in terms of scope and location to meet the most pressing system needs is a key feature of the
Flexibility Services program.

Toronto Hydro has not proposed its own local programs under the 2021-2024 CDM framework.
However, the utility continues to support programs delivered by IESO under the Local Initiatives
Program. This includes outreach and marketing support for programs such as Coolsaver,
BizEnergySaver, and the upcoming heat pump program. Given the effort and success of centrally
delivered CDM, at this time, Toronto Hydro is focused on building on and supporting the IESO’s
efforts rather than duplicating programs. Toronto Hydro remains open to collaborating on future
CDM programs with the IESO, and exploring opportunities for benefit-stacking where possible.
Toronto Hydro’s own efforts in the realm of demand-side management, focus on targeted and
credible opportunities where capital deferral or avoidance through non-wires solutions can be
identified and measured. This is based on a ground up analysis of system needs, and the targeted
deployment of demand-side management program called Local Demand Response (“LDR”), as
outlined in detail in the evidence at Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2.
1 This did not include certain stations (i.e. Dufferin TS, Terauley TS, Esplanade TS, Horner TS and Windsor TS)
for which projects carried over from 2020-2024. The work planned for these stations is described in Exhibit
2B, Section E5.3.

in Table 18 using different assumptions, including 50% of load transfer projects in scope are
avoided entirely while 50% are deferred for at least 5-years; and, if 100% of projects are
avoided entirely.

analysis following the OEB’s release of the draft BCA Framework. If Toronto Hydro has
conducted any analysis using the OEB’s BCA Framework examples, please provide.

calculate net present values, or if additional discount rates (e.g., social discount rate,

f) Please confirm that if successful, the LDR program will not require Toronto Hydro to raise
the capital required for the traditional wires solution, either in whole or in part, depending
on the level of transfer projects entirely avoided or deferred.
g) Please provide the factors and considerations that led Toronto Hydro to the conclusion
that the Shared Savings Mechanisms incentive options were not sufficient to level the
playing field between the LDR program and load transfers.

response:
The LDR program that is currently underway is targeting two stations, Manby TS and Horner TS. As
described on page 11 in Exhibit 2B Section E7.2, the consideration of LDR as an NWS has enabled
planners to avoid all incremental load transfers that would otherwise have been carried out in
order to manage Manby TS between 2022 and 2024.
This experience has confirmed that adding the consideration of NWSs to the load demand project
selection and scoping process introduces the opportunity to re-prioritize capital work. As a result,
in cases where the LDR can successfully be procured, load transfers that are intended to manage
capacity constraints during an interim period (prior to executing a permanent wires solution) can
be avoided.
Looking ahead at 2025-2029, as described in on pages 8 and 9 in Exhibit 2B Section E7.2, Toronto
Hydro is targeting 30 MW at a group of six stations. Each of these stations currently has an
estimated volume of load transfers that could materialize. The high range is 175 MVA and the low
range is 100 MVA. Based on the diversity of needs at these stations, it is not prudent to assume
that 100% of the load transfers targeted by the procurement of 30 MW of DR can be entirely
avoided. Engineering judgement was utilized to estimate that 75% could be avoided, while 25%
could be deferred. Note that this estimate, and the resulting BCA, provides a conceptual
understanding of the difference in value and benefit that arises in cases where capital is entirely
avoided versus capital being deferred. The figures could change based on the actual load demand
projects targeted, as well as the ability to procure DR capacity. This is to be expected when
considering the use of third-party owned, market-based solutions to address dynamic demand-
related system needs.

The analysis presented in the tables above aligns with Toronto Hydro’s understanding that capital
avoidance of load transfers constitutes the primary source of economic benefits for the LDR
program. At the same time, while deferral of load transfers may ultimately provide small (but
positive) economic benefits, this approach can provide operational flexibility to areas of grid that
face demand volatility or uncertainty. In these more dynamic circumstances that the utility could
be faced with in the next rate period as customers adopt new technologies, deferring load transfers
through LDR can be a prudent strategy even if the economic benefits are relatively small.
Postponement or deferral of load transfers “buys time” to let the uncertainty and volatility settle
before making the decision to undertake a load transfer investment that will add cost to the rate
base for many years. Postponement can also result in the decision to avoid the related capital
expenditures should it become apparent that such work is no longer needed.

Overall, the BCA methodology that Toronto Hydro applied is aligned with the draft BCA framework
released by the OEB. The largest source of diﬀerence is the ‘Pre-Assessment’ Criteria, which
Toronto Hydro addressed in its February 1, 2024 comments to the OEB in EB-2023-0125.1 Toronto
Hydro intends to continue to evolve its BCA methodology to maintain alignment with the OEB
framework as it evolves and takes shape.

WACC used for the BCA analysis is a nominal weighted average cost of capital, that includes
inflation. Assuming that inflation will be around 2% post 2025, the real WACC used for the BCA is
4.17%.

Toronto Hydro’s assessment of NWS benefits applies to distribution systems needs and value. Bulk
value assessments have not been included as part of Toronto Hydro’s DSP at this time, as there is
no established framework for capturing this value.

Confirmed for the proposed 2025-2029 program.

Please see the evidence in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1 at pages 53-54. To arrive at this conclusion,
Toronto Hydro assessed the foregone opportunity to earn a regulated rate of return (“ROE”) on the
capital investments avoided and deferred, using an NPV approach. The resulting analysis presented
in Table 18 of the evidence shows that the LDR target to procure 30MW results in foregone utility
ROE of approximately $3.2 million due to the deferral and avoidance of load transfer capital
expenditures. By comparison a 50:50 shared saving mechanism based on the calculated NPV of
benefits associated with the proposed target ($3.3 million) yields an incentive of approximately
$1.7 million. Compared to the foregone revenue of $3.2 million, and the operational and market
risk and complexity associated with a successful delivery of the LDR proposal, Toronto Hydro did
not find the shared savings outcome acceptable.

The LDR program’s success will be evaluated on the basis of capacity procured, cost of DR ($/MW-
day), capacity deployed, and avoided or deferred load transfers in each station area targeted by the
program. The methodology utilized in the BCA provided will be recalculated annually to evaluate
cumulative program success throughout the rate-period.

Consistent with the fixed incentive option outlined at page 8 of the OEB’s Filing Guidelines for
Incentives for Electricity Distributors to Use Third-Party DERs as Non-Wires Alternatives, Toronto
Hydro’s proposal is that the final incentive value will be based on actual versus forecast “amount
[MW] of system capacity provided by third-party owned DER solutions that would otherwise have to
be provided by a wires solution.”

response:
Please refer to Table 3 (Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, pages. 12 to 15) for a breakdown of key
investments contributing to the achievement of the Outage Duration performance target. Toronto
Hydro is unable to provide a specific list of projects that will contribute to successfully achieving the
target by the end of 2029, as those projects have yet to be planned, designed, and issued for
execution. Toronto Hydro typically issues detailed scopes of work for capital projects 12-18 months
ahead of construction.

Major Event Days (‘MEDs’) and outages caused by extreme weather are not one and the same. The
investments that Toronto Hydro plans to make to improve SAIDI will have benefits for outage
duration during adverse and extreme weather events, whether those events meet the statistical
classification threshold for MEDs or not.
As stated in the OEB’s RRR,1 “such [Major] events disrupt normal business operations and occur so
infrequently that it would be uneconomical to take them into account when designing and
operating the distribution system.” The IEEE 1366 standard2 clarifies the intended purpose of Major
Event Day classification is “to allow major events to be studied separately from daily operation, and
in the process, to better reveal trends in daily operation that would be hidden by the large
statistical effect of major events”. In essence, MEDs are a way of classifying statistical outlier events
that would otherwise obscure and distort average performance statistics. MEDs are inherently
difficult to predict, highly variable in their circumstances and outcomes, and not suited to reliability
performance target setting.
As stated in the evidence (Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, page 9), for the 2025-2029 period, Toronto
Hydro intends to improve Outage Duration performance as measured by the custom SAIDI metric
compared to historical performance. This objective aligns with customer needs and priorities
identified through Phase 1 of Toronto Hydro’s Customer Engagement which highlighted that when
it comes to reliability performance, all customers (except Key Accounts) prioritize reducing the
overall length of outages rather than the number of outages. For more information on the outputs
1 Ontario Energy Board: Electricity Reporting and Record Keeping Requirements (‘RRR’)
2 IEEE Std 1366-2022: IEEE Guide for Electric Power Distribution Reliability Indices
of the customer engagement process, in particular reliability priorities, please refer to Exhibit 1B,
Tab 5, Schedule 1, Appendix A at page 8).

As illustrated by the IRM scenario in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, at page 10, Toronto Hydro would
be unable to maintain historical performance of 48.2 (2018-2022 average) without incremental
investment. The reliability projection for Toronto Hydro’s proposed capital expenditure plan
suggests that the utility’s investment plan is only sufficient to maintain Outage Duration as
measured by the custom SAIDI metric over the 2025-2029 period. However, the utility challenged
itself to set a modest improvement target, recognizing the importance of outage duration to
customers when it comes to reliability performance as noted in part (a). As such, the entirety of the
2025-2029 Investment Plan (approximately $4.0 billion in capital and supporting OM&A
expenditures) is required to support expanding, modernizing and sustaining the foundations of the
grid and essential to managing Outage Duration performance in the next rate period.

Toronto Hydro notes that setting reliability targets on a five-year average basis is aligned with the
OEB’s Electricity Distributor Scorecard approach. Settling reliability targets on a five-year rolling
average basis is a common practice in the sector because it allows utilities to track performance
over a relatively short time frame while still smoothing out short-term fluctuations and providing a
reasonable basis for planning. Expanding the rolling average to 10-years presents several
challenges that makes it less valid:
•
Relevance of data: A 10-year rolling average includes data that is less relevant to current
conditions and technology standards.
•
Risk of masking recent trends and investment impacts: A 10-year rolling average smooths
out recent performance fluctuations to the extent that it can mask important trends or
issues that need immediate attention within the context of five-year investment planning.
It also increases the historical inertia in the measure from year-to-year, making it less
meaningful as performance incentive that can be influenced through actions taken in the
next five years.
•
Changing customer expectations: Customer expectations for reliability change over time
due to many factors. A 10-year rolling average may not capture these changing
expectations as effectively as a shorter time frame. Applying a 10-year rolling average
approach to Toronto Hydro’s data would result in a target that would represent significant
deterioration in reliability performance compared to the recent five-year average. This
outcome would not be aligned with the result of Toronto Hydro’s Customer Engagement.

question:
Toronto Hydro stated that to allow for updates of the annual inflation factor in rates without
double-counting the impact of inflation, Toronto Hydro adjusted the Revenue Growth Factor (RGF)
by removing a 2% forecasted annual inflation factor for the 2026 to 2029 period. Toronto Hydro
stated that it is presenting the RGF as an increase in revenue requirement, on an inflation-adjusted
basis for rate-setting purposes.
Toronto Hydro also noted that there is “current volatility in national and global inflation, which may
or may not subside over the 2025 to 2029 rate period.”
OEB staff notes that the Canadian consumer price index rose 3.4% in December from a year ago,
following a 3.1% increase a month earlier, as reported by Statistics Canada in January 2024.

a) Please explain the basis for the 2% forecasted annual inflation that will adjust the RGF.
b) Please explain how the 2% forecasted annual inflation relates to capital expenditures, gross
plant additions, and OM&A expenses.
c) Please explain why a higher amount than 2% to adjust the RGF may be more appropriate,
given that inflation remains trending in Canada at a rate greater than 3% and Toronto
Hydro also noted that inflation may not subside over its rate term.
response:
The 2% inflation that was applied to adjust the RGF/CRCI was based on the Bank of Canada’s
projection for inflation as presented in the quarterly monetary policy reports, which consistently
indicated throughout 2023 that inflation will reach the 2% target by the end of 2024 or middle of
2025.1 The actual inflation factor that Toronto Hydro proposes to apply in the CRCI during the annual
1 https://www.bankofcanada.ca/publications/mpr/
rate update applications (i.e. 2021-2024) is the OEB’s annually published Inflation Factor, made up
of 70% GDP-IPI-FDD and 30% Ontario Average Weekly Earnings.2

The 2% inflation factor referenced above is a rate-making mechanism for the purposes of establishing
an index (i.e., the CRCI) that can be applied to set rates mechanistically during the outer years of the
rate period (i.e., 2026 to 2029). This approach is consistent with standard incentive regulation before
the OEB which relies on broad indices (rather than bottom-up cost forecasts) to capture variances in
costs driven by business market conditions.
For planning purposes (i.e. to forecast the capital expenditures and OM&A expenses outlined in
Exhibits 2B and 4 that form the revenue requirement presented in Exhibit 6), Toronto Hydro relied
on different assumptions for the different components of the plan:
•
Internal labour costs: Forecasting for these costs was based on existing negotiated labour
agreements. In cases where there are no existing agreements for certain groups of
employees, Toronto Hydro relied on historical rolling forecast to estimate future labour-
related costs.
•
Non-Labour Related Costs: These costs were estimated assuming an annual 2% inflationary
increase over the 2026-2029 period.
2 In 1B-Staff-93, Toronto Hydro withdrew its request for a custom labour component for the inflation factor.

Toronto Hydro does not believe that a higher amount would be more appropriate because the Bank
of Canada’s latest monetary policy report, issued in January 2024, continues to note that “[t]he Bank
projects that inflation will stay around 3% through the first half of 2024, returning to [the 2%] target
in 2025.” In any event, applying a higher amount to adjust the RGF at this stage of the rate-setting
process leads to the same outcome on a forecast basis since the proposed RGF has been inflation
adjusted so that the actual inflation factor prevailing at the time of the annual rate update can be
added back in to set rates for the upcoming year. Table 3 of the Rate Framework evidence at Exhibit
1B, Tab 2, Schedule 1 at page 25 (reproduced below for ease of reference) sets this out:

which it has proposed a 5% overall weight, includes the proposed activities to electrify 50%
of its fleet and reduce GHG emissions at its work centers by 3% each year.

incremental annual target and that by 2029, a minimum GHG emissions reduction of 15%

Confirmed.

question:
Regarding stated investments to improve SAIDI and SAIFI in the above referenced sections.

a) Are Toronto Hydro’s historical investments in grid sensor, remote-operable switches, smart
meters and SCADA controlled switches (advancing “self-healing” grid operations) the
primary drivers for the improvements achieved in SAIDI and SAIFI since 2013?
i.
If not, what are the primary drivers of the improvements?
ii.
If yes, please discuss the impact that continued investment in these activities at the
same pace will have on improvements in SAIDI and SAIFI results.
b) Please compare the historic and forecast substantial reliability improvements in SAIDI and
SAIFI achieved by Toronto Hydro with the improvements reported by the US Department
of Energy for utilities that implemented FLISR.
c) Are the forecast substantial incremental reliability improvements “three to seven percent
for SAIFI and four to seven percent for SAIDI on the overhead system”?
i.
If not, what are the forecast substantial incremental reliability improvements for
SAIDI and SAIFI?
response:
Out of the technologies listed in the question, only remote-operable switches (which are the same
as SCADA controlled switches) have had a material impact on reliability since 2013. Specifically, these
switches have had a positive impact on SAIDI. Remote operable switches require operator
intervention, meaning that they do not typically result in reductions in the frequency of sustained
interruptions, and therefore do not have a material impact on SAIFI. As noted in Exhibit 2B, Section
E7.1.3.1, page 7, analysis of 2018-2022 reliability data shows that the average duration for outages
on feeders with less than three SCADA tie-points was approximately 707 minutes per year per feeder,
whereas the average duration of those feeders with three or more SCADA tie-points was
approximately 496 minutes. As part of Toronto Hydro’s reliability projections for 2025-2029, the
utility quantified estimated improvements from SCADA switch installations (see response to
interrogatory 2B-SEC-42 for more details).
Regarding the other technologies referenced in the question, Toronto Hydro has not broadly
deployed grid sensors, except within its network system (see Exhibit 2B, Section E7.3 for details and
benefits), and its existing, first-generation smart meters do not possess “last gasp” technology,
meaning that they do not have the capabilities to assist with outage restoration efforts.
(i)
Regarding the primary drivers of reliability improvement in the historical period, in
addition to the relevant modernization investments discussed above, Toronto Hydro’s
System Renewal and System O&M investments have been foundational to mitigating
asset risk, eliminating obsolete assets and system configurations, and ultimately
improving both SAIDI and SAIFI performance since 2013. For additional details on
Toronto Hydro’s historical performance from 2018 to 2023, please see Exhibit 2B,
Section C.

To clarify, Toronto Hydro has not yet implemented automated FLISR, nor is Toronto Hydro
anticipating benefits from automated FLISR during the 2025-2029 period. For longer-term reliability
improvements pertaining to automated FLISR, please refer to the response to 2B-Staff-162.

The percentages referenced are associated with the forecasted improvements at the end of the
2025-2029 period upon the completion of additional SCADA switches and new mid-line recloser
installations, as described in the System Enhancements program (Exhibit 2B, Section E7.1).
For longer-term reliability improvements pertaining to Fault Location Isolation and Service
Restoration (“FLISR”), also referred to as Distribution Automation (“DA”), please refer to Toronto
Hydro’s response to interrogatory 2B-Staff-162.

question:
In its description of innovation over the 2020 to 2024 rate period, Toronto Hydro describes its
approach to building innovative strategies across numerous dimensions of its business including
the creation of an Innovation Sandbox.

a) Please explain how Toronto Hydro funded its Innovation Sandbox, how it measured success
of the initiatives and provide additional details on which initiatives have been scaled into
normal operations.
b) Outside of its sandbox, please explain how Toronto Hydro determines what innovative pilots
it will fund and how it assesses when an initiative is ready for scale?
c) Please explain how Toronto Hydro determines which initiatives fall under the heading of
innovation and why this isn’t considered a part of normal utility management. For example,
under System Observability: Network Condition, Monitoring and Control (1.2 of above noted
scheduled), Toronto Hydro references how it continues to advance its Network Condition
Monitoring and Control to increase situational awareness the low voltage distribution
network.
d) Please explain how the areas in which Toronto Hydro plans to test specific new distribution
capabilities in the upcoming rate period differ from the areas explored and funded previously
by Toronto Hydro in the current rate period (during which it did not have an Innovation
Fund).
e) Please explain why Toronto Hydro requires both the support of the Future Energy Scenarios
tool as well as the Innovation Fund to stress test grid modernization investments in the 2025-
2029 rate period.
f) The four pilot areas tagged for the Innovation Fund were identified as part of the Grid
Modernization Strategy in reference 3. What focus areas of the strategy do they fall under
and can Toronto Hydro please explain why they can't be incorporated into the initiatives
already planned?
g) Please provide any additional analysis of comparable jurisdictions innovation funding
amounts, other than those included in the application (i.e., Ofgem, New York, Enbridge Gas).
h) Please provide more details regarding the proposed governance framework, including titles
and responsibilities of the steering committee members, anticipated timelines for review of
each project, how innovation projects will be staffed (e.g., will existing staff people be
leveraged, will new FTEs be dedicated to pilot project owner roles, etc.), and if Toronto Hydro
proposes to keep the OEB and industry updated on its progress so opportunities and lessons
learned can be considered.
i)
Please discuss the likelihood of the innovation fund exceeding the requested $16M. If so,
what mechanisms does Toronto Hydro propose be put in place to ensure that any
additional funding is appropriate and will provide benefits to ratepayers.
response:
The Innovation Sandbox was self-funded by Toronto Hydro over the 2020-2024 rate period. Success
of pilot projects developed through Toronto Hydro’s Innovation Sandbox is assessed against a set of
criteria that is determined as a part of project approval prior to launch. If deemed successful upon
completion of proof-of-concept, the project is recommended for full-scale adoption.
Descriptions of projects that have been tested through the Innovation Sandbox and scaled into
normal operations can be found at Exhibit 1B, Tab 4, Schedule 1 at pages 2-3.

Outside of the Sandbox, Toronto Hydro has proposed an Innovation Fund, along with an associated
Governance Framework, which is described in Exhibit 1B, Tab 4, Schedule 2.

As outlined in Exhibit 1B, Tab 4, Schedule 1 and Schedule 2 at page 4, initiatives under the heading
of innovation are designed to test new technologies, advanced capabilities, and alternative strategies
that are more early stage, exploratory and developmental in nature. These explorations can lead to
innovation that is then scaled up into normal utility operations. The Network Condition Monitoring
and Control (NCMC) initiative exemplifies this approach. Initially conceived as an innovation project,
NCMC has proven successful and has since been integrated into Toronto Hydro’s standard utility
operations. Furthermore the insights gained, skills honed, and benefits realized through the NCMC
program have led to the continued implementation of system observability technologies, as outlined
in the Grid Modernization Strategy detailed in Exhibit 2B, Section D5, and summarized in Exhibit 1B,
Tab 4, Schedule 1 at section 2.1.

The internal sandbox was launched to engage and encourage employees to bring forward ideas for
proof-of-concept projects that are novel and provide value to customers across all areas of the
company’s business and processes. This initiative empowers employees to embrace change and
fosters a culture of innovation, meaning a solution-oriented mindset that obstacles can be overcome
through creative problem-solving. Please refer to Exhibit 1B, Tab 4, Schedule 01, Section 1.1 for more
details on about the internal Sandbox.
The proposed Innovation Fund represents a more targeted approach to the innovation that is
required to address the fundamental changes in the energy landscape and manage the uncertainty
driven by the imperatives of decarbonizing key sectors of the economy through electrification.
Particularly in response to expectations set by the Ontario Energy Board (OEB) regarding Distributed
Energy Resource (DER) integration, as outlined in the Framework for Energy Innovation (FEI) report.
The Innovation Fund addresses needs that are not adequately met by existing funding mechanisms.
In this way, the Innovation Fund would be complementary to existing funding mechanisms insofar
as they relate to innovation.
Key differentiators for the Innovation Fund supported projects include an emphasis on adapting
operational practices to manage DERs effectively, modifying planning processes to incorporate non-
utility-owned DER solutions, and prioritizing the development of skills and knowledge within the
organization.
Additionally, the projects under the Innovation Fund are expected to deploy inventive solutions
aligned with the OEB's definition of innovation, focusing on leveraging new technologies, innovative
business practices, and enhancing distribution services for the benefit of customers. This strategic
alignment ensures that Toronto Hydro remains at the forefront of industry advancements and
delivers value to stakeholders. Please refer to Exhibit 1B, Tab 4, Schedule 02, Section 3 for more
details on Areas of Innovation.

The Future Energy Scenarios is a model that was created to help Toronto Hydro understand possible
changes to future peak demand under different scenarios, and was used to stress-test whether the
utility’s capacity plan can accommodate energy transition needs (e.g. building heating electrification)
in the early part of the next decade, if required.
The Future Energy Scenarios inform possible grid modernization investments as they relate to the
various scenarios. For more information, please refer to Exhibit 2B Section D4.
The proposed Innovation Fund is funding mechanism for exploring innovative capabilities that can
help Toronto Hydro better adapt to fundamental changes taking place in the energy system as a
result of the transition, by leveraging technology to achieve expanded benefits for customers. It is
an important part of Toronto Hydro’s approach to innovation because it addresses needs that are
not adequately met by existing funding mechanisms. For more information, please refer to Exhibit
1B Tab 4 Schedule 2.
In summary, the Future Energy Scenarios is a tool for planning and conceptualizing innovative
approaches relating to peak demand management, while the Innovation Fund provides the
necessary funding to scope, design and execute innovative pilot projects.

The four pilot projects (as described in Exhibit 2B Section D5 Appendix I) would fall under the Grid
Readiness focus area of the Grid Modernization Strategy. However, these projects are distinct from
other initiatives which are proposed in the Grid Readiness focus area, which Toronto Hydro proposes
would be funded through normal mechanisms as they may be deployed as standard distribution
system solutions or IT projects. Whereas existing mechanisms tend to support spending where the
beneficial outcomes are more proven or certain, the proposed Innovation Fund would be able to
support work that is more early stage, exploratory and developmental in nature. The four pilot
project concepts fall into this earlier stage and exploratory category and were considered to be too
nascent to deploy as standard distribution system solutions. They were also identified as posing a
funding risk because more developmental work is needed to test the technologies and prove related
beneficial outcomes for Toronto Hydro’s system.
It is important to note that funding these pilot project ideas through the Innovation Fund would allow
Toronto Hydro to determine the funding implications in real time based on the facts of each project
or initiative. Thereby, Toronto Hydro would be able to design and implement pilot projects and other
exploratory initiatives more effectively.

Please refer to Toronto Hydro’s response to interrogatory 1B-DRC-06 part (d).

Please see Toronto Hydro’s response to interrogatory 1B-DRC-06 part (i).

Toronto Hydro cannot speculate on the likelihood of actual expenditures exceeding the requested
funding amount since it has not commenced the pilot selection and design phases of the Governance
Framework, which is where the projects will be scoped, and workplan and budgets created. For
further discussion, please refer to Toronto Hydro’s response to interrogatory 1B-CCC-46 part (h).

question: a) How was the 0.6 ($65 million) value for PIM amount chosen?
response:
Toronto Hydro applied the following key considerations in the decision to include a 0.6% incentive-
factor attributed to the PIM in the proposed custom rate framework:
•
The OEB’s expectation in the Rate Handbook that the X-Factor included in a custom index
should be higher than X-Factor that would otherwise be assigned under Price Cap IR.
Together the efficiency-factor of 0.15% and the PIM of 0.6%, Toronto Hydro’s proposed
X-Factor is 0.75%, which is 0.15% greater than the X-factor under Price Cap IR;
•
The principle and objective of balancing the utility risk/reward under the PIM with the

question:
“As the sub-metering market has become more mature in Toronto over the last decade, a greater
share of new multi-unit buildings is opting for bulk-metering service connections. The practical
effect of operating in this urban environment with a deregulated sub-metering market is a slower
rate of formally reported customer growth from 2013 to 2022, which is putting artificial
upward pressure on cost performance metrics like Total Cost Per Customer and Total Cost per km
of Line.”

a) Does THESL provide sub-metering services in competition with other service providers in
Ontario?
b) If yes, are any sub-metering costs included in this application for recovery from
ratepayers?
It is unclear to us why sub-metering would result in higher costs per customers. For example,
presumably THESL avoids the cost of individual metering, meter reading, line connection and other
high-cost activities associated with individual metered customers. Conversely bulk metered
customers are a lower cost to serve. The result would be that while the number of residential units
is increasing in the average costs to THESL of serving those customers is also decreasing. In any
event, what evidence/studies does THESL have to demonstrate that sub-metering (all
other things being equal) results in a higher, rather than lower, or unchanged cost per customer?
A similar insinuation of costs per customer is made at Schedule 3 which notes that Toronto Hydro
provides an average of 31.8 MWh per customer, more load per customer relative to the peer group
of utilities who have a multi-year average of 23.6 MWh. The evidence ascribes this relative difference
to the proliferation of high rises. However, it is not clear why this is a relevant consideration if one
assumes that there is a lower cost of delivered power for utilities with a greater proportion of bulk
metered units. Please provide the studies that THESL relies upon to support its contention that
higher density of customers is a more costly delivery model than lower density service.
response:
No. In accordance with Part III of the Energy Consumer Protection Act, 2010, Toronto Hydro provides
services as a unit smart meter provider, meaning a distributor licensed by the Board to engage in
unit smart metering. The utility does not engage in competitive unit sub-metering activities related
to multi-unit complexes that are connected to a bulk meter. The evidence referenced above notes
that as the unit sub-metering market has become more mature, a greater share of the multi-unit
buildings being constructed are opting for a Toronto Hydro bulk meter service (with competitive unit
sub-metering), rather than a Toronto Hydro unit smart metering service.

The referenced evidence is not an assertion about the relative cost of serving bulk metered vs.
individually metered customers. Rather, it is about the prevalence of unit sub-metering in Toronto
Hydro’s service territory skewing comparative metrics that use customer count as the denominator.
Unit sub-metering results in the aggregation of dozens or hundreds of end-consumers behind a single
bulk-meter, and subsequently counts each multi-unit building with a bulk-meter as a single customer.
As noted in the OM&A Overview evidence at Exhibit 4, Tab 1, Schedule 1 at page 11, Toronto Hydro
estimates that it serves approximately 340,000 end-consumers or more behind bulk meters.

Operating in a dense urban environment drives unique challenges which have an impact on costs as
evidenced in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 3 at pages 2-8 and in the Total Cost Benchmarking Study
found at Appendix A of the same reference.
The referenced analysis illustrates a key operational difference between the utility and its Ontario
peers that should be considered when evaluating cost per customer benchmarks. Because Toronto
Hydro has substantially more high-rise buildings than comparator utilities in Ontario, its customer
count denominator is lower than it otherwise would be if that number included sub-metered
residential customers in buildings serviced by a bulk-metered. As a result it is not unreasonable to
see in the cost per customer benchmarking analyses that Toronto Hydro has more demand, more
consumption, more net fixed assets, and more OM&A cost per customer compared to its peers.
For a specific discussion of how serving a dense service territory relates to asset utilization and costs,
please see Toronto Hydro’s response to 2B-Staff-121.
