Regarding Toronto Hydro’s forecasted DER penetration, DER caused potential complexity to system
operations, and DER hosting and load capacity map.

a) Please provide Toronto Hydro’s DER connection policies that are being put into place to
limit the complexity and instability caused by DERs?
b) Is Toronto Hydro implementing policies to incentivize DER development in areas where the
grid has excess capacity, and disincentivize DERs in areas with restricted capacity?
i.
If yes, please provide documentation.
ii.
If no, please explain why this is prudent from a ratepayer and legislative
perspective.
c) Who bears the cost of expenditures needed to enable DER connections on feeders that do
not have excess hosting capacity?
i.
Why is this prudent from a ratepayer perspective?
d) Does the Hosting Capacity Analysis (HCA) discourage or otherwise inhibit potential DER
candidates from connecting to the grid in areas that have capacity constraints? Please
discuss.
i.
If not, what is the value to ratepayers of the expenditures required for the HCA?
response:
Toronto Hydro has clear DER connections guidelines, as outlined in Toronto Hydro’s Conditions of
Service Reference 3 document. By following these guidelines and working with its customers
through the DER Connections process, Toronto Hydro ensures that safety, technical and operating
requirements are satisfied with respect to DER connections. This helps the utility manage potential
complexities that may be introduced to the grid.

Toronto Hydro supports DER connections in accordance with the Distribution System Code (DSC) and
plans to incent DER development by providing customers with better visibility and essential
information regarding available capacity (Hosting Capacity Assessment and Maps – Exhibit 2B,
Section D5.3.4) so that customers can be well informed about system constraints when planning
their DER projects. In addition, through an expanded Local Demand Response initiative as part of the
Non-Wires Solution program (Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2) Toronto Hydro continues to offer financial
incentives (i.e. capacity payments) for DER resources that can offer demand response services to the
grid. This offering includes the development of online DR Capacity Auction tool to make it easier for
customers and aggregators to participate in Local DR.

In accordance with section 3.3.3 of the DSC, system enhancements costs are borne by the distributor
rather than by individual customers. Distribution investments to connect, or enable the connection,
of Renewable Energy Generation (“REG”) facilities to Toronto Hydro’s distribution system are eligible
for provincial rate recovery under section 79.1 of the Ontario Energy Board Act, 1998. Please see
Exhibit 2A, Tab 5, Schedule 1 for more information.

Yes. A public-facing HCA map or data portal can potentially discourage DER candidates from
connecting to the grid in areas with capacity constraints. This is because the map may show that
the local grid cannot support additional DERs without significant upgrades or modifications.
Knowing this, potential candidates might choose not to invest in DERs in these areas due to the
anticipated costs, delays, or uncertainties associated with grid upgrades.
Conversely, a HCA map can also empower DER candidates by providing them with preliminary
information about the grid’s capacity. This transparency enables them to make more informed
decisions regarding where and how to invest in DER technologies. For example, they might decide
to install DER in areas with more capacity or consider smaller systems that fit the existing grid
capabilities.

question:
Toronto Hydro states that a U.S. Department of Energy report on FLISR implement found that
“FLISR reduced the number of Cis (“Customers Interrupted”) by up to 45 percent and reduced the
CMIs (“Customer Minutes of Interruption”) by up to 51 percent for a relevant outage event.” The
footnote indicates that the time basis of calculating momentary outages in the study is different
than that used by Toronto Hydro.

a) Please quantify the reported improvement in Toronto Hydro’s FLISR metrics if Toronto
Hydro uses the same metric definition as in the U.S. Department of Energy Study.
b) Please update Table 11 in Reference 2 (PDF Page 364/1113) based on using the same
definition of SAIFI for Toronto Hydro and its peers.
response:
As detailed in Exhibit 2B, Section D5.2.1.2, Toronto Hydro anticipates substantial benefits from the
introduction of automatic FLISR starting in 2030. See response to interrogatory 2B-Staff-162, part
(a) for anticipated benefits of a full-scale implementation of FLISR across the Horseshoe Region.
It is important to note that the level of benefits achieved from automatic FLISR will ultimately
depend on the specific technical and operating realities with respect to integrating FLISR into
Toronto Hydro’s existing distribution system. The utility will have a more accurate expectation of
likely benefits once it has made substantial progress on the “manual FLISR” implementation
planned for the 2025-2029 rate period.
The maximum benefits cited from the U.S. Department of Energy report were derived from feeder-
level data collected from 266 FLISR events observed over the course of a year. By comparison,
Toronto Hydro evaluated the expected impact of FLISR on its system-wide reliability statistics,
meaning that the benefits are statistically diluted by including outages that would not be impacted
by FLISR (see 2B-Staff-162 for more information).

Please note the reliability benchmarking results provided in Table 11, and others in the Reliability
Benchmarking Study prepared by Clearspring Energy Advisors, are based on different interruption
reporting practices, which are not applied to Toronto Hydro and other distributors in Ontario.
Most notably, Toronto Hydro and its peer distributors in Ontario and across Canada follow a one-
minute threshold for sustained interruptions, which differs from the predominant five-minute
interruption definition used in the US for sustained interruptions, as detailed in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3,
Schedule 3, App A, Pg. 25. Based on available data, Toronto Hydro is not able to reproduce Table 11
on a one-minute sustained interruption threshold, however, in order to maintain consistency with
the benchmarking approach, it provided its interruption data on a 5-minute sustained interruption
threshold, which underpins the information provided in Table 11.

question:
Toronto Hydro states “In the current rate period, Toronto Hydro’s operating parameters shifted
from a relatively linear and stable environment to a more dynamic growth-oriented context.”

a) Please reconcile the statement above with the negative Total Normalized MVA (% change),
and Total Normalized GWh (% change) as shown in Table 5 in Reference 2.
b) Is the described shift in operating parameters from “linear and stable” to “more dynamic
growth-oriented” a key driver of Toronto Hydro’s step-increase in overall capital spending
relative to historical spending?
c) Does the shift from “linear and stable” to “more dynamic growth-oriented” materially
affect the pace of renewal spending? If yes, please explain why.
response:
Reference 1 refers to significant increases in future customer demand driven by an unprecedented
energy transition that is creating new and expanded roles for electricity within the economy. To
gain insight into the challenge posed by the energy transition, Toronto Hydro commissioned an
industry leading consumer-choice modelling Future Energy Scenarios study to assess the impacts of
different energy transition scenarios on Toronto Hydro’s distribution system. The Future Energy
Scenarios study (filed in Exhibit 2B, Section D3) reveals that in the next two-three decades, a
significant increase in peak demand across all scenarios is expected to occur, including the least
ambitious steady progression scenario that falls short of meeting Net Zero 2050 objectives. This
outlook is consistent with other leading studies, such as the Independent Electricity System
Operator’s (“IESO”) Pathways to Decarbonization (“P2D”) report, which estimates that in a high-
growth scenario, in less than 30 years, Ontario could need more than double its electricity
generating capacity.
Reference 2 refers to Toronto Hydro load forecast for billing purposes in the 2025-2029 rate term.
Please see response to 1B-PP-18 for the further details.

As noted in Exhibit 2B, Section A at page 2, investing in the performance and long-term viability of
an aged, deteriorated, and highly utilized system, while preparing the system to meet the demands
of increased electrification, is a key priority of Toronto Hydro’s 2025-2029 Distribution System Plan.
As noted in Exhibit 2B, Section E4.2 on page 15, compared to the current 2020-2024 rate period,
there is a shift in the 2025-2029 rate period towards System Access and System Service investments
to:
i)
keep pace with the demands of customers in a city that is growing, digitizing and
decarbonizing its economy, and
ii)
prepare the grid for the energy transition that is set to unfold over the next two decades
by modernizing the utility’s infrastructure and operations to improve resiliency, enable
DER integration and deliver long-term reliability and efficiency benefits to customers.
Please see Exhibit 2B, Section E4 starting on page 15 for a detailed summary of forecast (2025-2029)
vs. historical (2020-2024) expenditures by investment category.

When normalized for inflation, the pace of renewal investment in the next rate period is increasing
by approximately 25% compared to historical investment levels (see 2B-Staff-69). As summarized in
Exhibit 2B, Section E4.2.2 at page 17, this increase is necessary to manage significant safety,
reliability, and environmental asset risks, maintain the system in a state of good repair by managing
the overall health demographics of assets, and ensure stable and predictable grid performance for
current and future customers. Expansion of capacity as part of renewal projects is not a major
incremental driver of the proposed level of System Renewal expenditures in this rate filing.
However, Toronto Hydro expects that the shift to a more dynamic growth-oriented context could
place incremental pressures on the System Renewal programs and influence the way renewal
projects are prioritized. The utility expects that accommodating neighbourhood-level growth due
to electrification will require upgrading the capacity of primary cables and conductors, distribution
transformers, secondary buses, and protection schemes, which in turn could have cascading effects
such as the need to accelerate voltage conversion projects. When Toronto Hydro replaces an asset
or rebuilds an area as part of a planned renewal project, it examines the demand in the area to
determine whether the new equipment should be built to a larger standard and whether the
feeder more broadly requires reconfiguration or load balancing. In a high electrification scenario, a
greater share of the allotted System Renewal funding will need to go toward these expansionary
costs, in turn reducing the extent to which expenditures are targeted more narrowly at mitigating
asset failure risk. In the long-term, Toronto Hydro cannot neglect asset deterioration and asset
failure risk, as this would lead to worsening reliability, heightened safety and environmental risks,
and an overall backlog of deteriorating assets that would need to be addressed at higher costs in
the future. Therefore, in the long-term, under a high electrification scenario, the utility expects the
dual drivers of reliability and growth to result in a higher overall need for System Renewal
investment.

Toronto Hydro states “Sustainment and Stewardship: Risk-based investments in the renewal of
aging, deteriorating and obsolete distribution equipment to maintain the foundations of a safe and
reliable gird.”

a) Toronto Hydro is proposing to increase its renewal spending by 35% relative to historical
levels (reference 2). Please explain the extent to which this overall increase is being driven
by any of the following factors:
•
changes in the rate of deterioration of Toronto Hydro’s assets
•
a backlog in historically unaddressed renewal needs
•
a change in the deemed acceptable failure risk threshold for specific asset types
•
other reasons.
b) Please provide a copy of Toronto Hydro’s internal distribution system planning process and
identify how it addresses non-wires solutions. What are the planned changes to the
planning process to better address identified non-wires objectives as per References 3 and
4.
c) In the present application did Toronto Hydro evaluate Non-Wires Solutions whenever
existing traditional “wires” assets (such as poles, conductor systems, underground cable,
transformers, switchgear, etc.) were identified as requiring replacement?
i.
If yes, please provide documentation of some representative evaluations that have
been undertaken.
ii.
If no, please explain why not, considering the recent guidance in References 3 and
4.
response:
Toronto Hydro continues to face asset demographic challenges in operating a mature distribution
system. As summarized in Exhibit 2B, Section A3.1, both condition and age demographics identify a
number of critical asset classes with significant investment needs over the 2025-2029 period. These
needs are driven by various factors, including those listed in the question above. Through its
investments in Sustainment and Stewardship, Toronto Hydro is aiming to maintain reliability and
asset risk current levels. Toronto Hydro has not materially changed its risk threshold for any major
asset classes from the previous rate period. However, as part of the utility’s strategy for improving
resiliency in parts of the overhead system that are critical and vulnerable to increased adverse
weather, Toronto Hydro has reintroduced an Overhead Infrastructure Resiliency segment to allow
for targeted relocation and undergrounding (Exhibit 2B, Section E6.5), and this partially explains
the increase in the Overhead System Renewal program compared to 2020-2024.
The following paragraphs provide a brief summary of the three major drivers of increases in the
System Renewal category: inflation; overhead and underground system health and reliability; and
asset deterioration in stations.
Inflation
As discussed and illustrated in Exhibit 2B, Section D2.1.3, and as reflected in the unit cost pressures
noted in other interrogatory responses (e.g., 2B-Staff-212), Toronto Hydro has dealt with significant
inflationary pressures in the current rate period. Calculating the actual amount by which labour and
materials inflation has impacted historical costs at the project level is a data-intensive undertaking.
However, using the OEB’s inflation factor, in combination with Toronto Hydro’s forward-looking
inflation assumptions, to adjust all of the expenditures in the 2020-2029 period to 2020 dollars, the
utility estimates that 60% of the increase in System Renewal expenditures is due to inflation.1
Overhead and Underground System Health and Reliability
The condition of Toronto Hydro’s overhead and underground systems has deteriorated since 2018.
As shown in Table 2 in Exhibit 2B, Section E2, the percentage of assets on the overhead system that
are in HI4/HI5 condition has increased from 6% to 9%. While the underground system percentage is
stable at 3%, the projected rate of deterioration is higher looking out to 2029 as compared to the
equivalent analysis done in 2018 (i.e., seven percentage points vs. four percentage points of
1 Toronto Hydro applied the 2021-2023 OEB inflation factors to 2020-2022. The OEB’s inflation factors lag
actual inflation by approximately two years.
deterioration without investment). Toronto Hydro also notes that the most critical asset on the
underground system from a reliability perspective is primary cable. This asset class is not reflected
in the condition models, and as discussed in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.2, Toronto Hydro has seen a
deterioration in reliability performance for this asset type during this rate period, with customer
interruptions increasing from a previous low of 105,000 in 2019 to 199,000 in 2022. For more
information, please refer to 2B-Staff-211.
Deterioration in asset condition and performance is partly related to the deferral of volumes of
work from the 2020-2024 period. This deferral was the result of inflationary pressures, as well as
the need to constrain expenditures in the major renewal programs as a means of balancing-out
unanticipated cost pressures from demand-related programs. This is discussed in Exhibit 2B,
Section E4.1. In recent years (and continuing through 2025), Toronto Hydro has also been focused
on removing transformers at risk of containing PCBs from its overhead and underground systems,
and this has diminished the utility’s ability to target assets and areas of the system in the worst
condition and most at risk of failure.
The Horseshoe area renewal programs are the capital programs that have the most significant
impact on the day-to-day reliability of the grid. Toronto Hydro has proposed the minimum pace of
investment necessary to manage asset risk and maintain reliability performance over the 2025-
2029 period. For full details on the programs, please refer to Exhibit 2B, Sections E6.2 and E6.5 For
more information on drivers of increases in the Overhead System Renewal program, please refer to
2B-Staff-219. For a comprehensive discussion on expected changes in asset demographics as a
result of Toronto Hydro’s 2025-2029 investment plan, please refer to 2B-SEC-44.
Asset Deterioration in Stations
Toronto Hydro also intends to accelerate its investment in the Stations Renewal program beyond
the pace set during the 2020-2024 period by 61%. This is in response to a considerable backlog of
aging and deteriorating assets, with the goal of securing the long-term reliability performance of
these critical asset populations. Table 2 in Toronto Hydro’s response to 2B-SEC-44 highlights the
condition demographics for key station assets. Additionally, the program is experiencing rising unit
costs for MS Switchgear, Power Transformers, and MS Primary Supply projects. For more detailed
information on the expenditure increases within the Stations Renewal program, refer to Exhibit 2B,
Section E6.6.

Toronto Hydro’s capacity planning process involves a ground up analysis of system capacity needs,
driven by load forecasts, as described in Exhibit 2B, Section D4. Planners pre-screen the types of
needs that could reliably be addressed by non-wires solutions based on credible opportunities to
defer or avoid capital investment through procurement of non-wires capacity. This pre-screening is
based on the size of the capacity need and the ability for Toronto Hydro to aggregate sufficient
quantities of dispatchable demand response (DR) to meet this need. For example, granular feeder-
level issues are difficult to address using NWS, as the total capacity of dispatchable DR on an
individual feeder is rarely sizeable enough to meet the need. On the other hand, station level issues
are often driven by capacity requirements that are too large to be reliably and cost-effectively met
through DR.
Where appropriate use cases have been identified, the planning process includes a consideration of
non-wires solutions at the options analysis phase. Figure 1 below provides a high-level summary of
this process.
Figure 1. High-level Schematic of Toronto Hydro’s Planning Process
Based on experience over the last two rate periods, Toronto Hydro’s identified use case of non-
wires solutions focuses on capital deferral or avoidance of bus-level load transfers, which can be
achieved through the procurement of dispatchable demand response from aggregators or
customers. Toronto Hydro also assesses non-wires solutions as alternatives to Station Expansion, as
illustrated in the Downsview TS business case at Exhibit 2B, Section E7.2 Appendix A, and discussed
in the response to 2B-Staff-253.
In accordance with the use case and the guidance in Reference 3, Toronto Hydro set an ambitious
target to procure 30MW of non-wires capacity to defer or avoid approximately 25% of the load
transfers that would otherwise be required at the targeted stations in the next rate term. As the
NWS market matures, and the ability the procure reliable DER services increases, Toronto Hydro
will continue evolve its planning process to identify and develop other credible use cases of non-
wires solutions. Please see the responses to 1B-Staff-88 and 1B-Staff-89 for more information.

response:
Yes. While there is no single “value […] per dollars spent” metric, Toronto Hydro undertakes business
case evaluations and expected benefits analyses for modernization projects at the appropriate stage
prior to release of funding.1 The exact form of these analyses will vary depending on the type of
1 Note that for its full-scale programmatic system investments, including segments within the System

question:
Toronto Hydro states that: “Toronto Hydro strives to maintain and improve reliability at local,
feeder-wide, and system-wide levels by continuously optimizing its system and deploying cost-
effective technologies and solutions.”
Question (A):
a) Does Toronto Hydro quantitatively evaluate its reliability investments to determine if they
are cost neutral or cost reducing?
i.
If yes, please provide some representative benefit-cost analyses.
ii.
If no, please explain how Toronto Hydro determines that its proposed reliability
improvement investments are benefit-cost effective.
b) Has Toronto Hydro identified unacceptable reliability trends relative to its historical
performance or its peers? Please explain.
i.
If no, is Toronto Hydro only undertaking reliability improvement investments that
are either cost neutral or cost reducing?
response:
Toronto Hydro is unclear as to what is meant by “cost neutral or cost reducing” in the context of
“reliability investments.” Investments to maintain or improve reliability are typically evaluated
through a “least cost” lens. This involves identifying the most cost-effective solutions to achieve
desired reliability levels. It prioritizes investments that provide the greatest reliability
improvements for the lowest cost. Toronto Hydro achieves this through its outcomes-oriented,
programmatic approach to investment planning, which is driven by customer needs and
preferences. The utility has a diverse portfolio of established investments across its System
Renewal and Service programs which contribute to reliability performance. Through the
Investment Planning & Portfolio Reporting process, the utility assesses trade-offs across investment
programs and develops an overall expenditure plan that is calibrated within given financial
constraints to deliver the best achievable reliability outcomes across relevant time horizons. Note
that cost, (including cost-savings from new technology) is a factor in this “least cost” investment
planning approach. However, cost is treated as its own variable to be optimized through the
planning process. This is achieved by (i) constraining the investment plan within budget
parameters, and (ii) updating bottom-up capital and operational cost assumptions to ensure
savings from past and future technology deployments are embedded in expenditure plans each
year. An example of this would be the operational savings from deploying Network Condition
Monitoring & Control technology, which have been embedded in future expenditure plan
assumptions for the relevant maintenance program. (See Exhibit 2B, Section E7.3, page 12 for more
information.)
As discussed in Section D1.2.1.1, as part of its ongoing multi-year effort to implement an industry
leading Engineering Asset Investment Planning (“EAIP”) platform, Toronto Hydro is developing a
custom value framework which assigns relative value to investments based on their likely
contribution to Toronto Hydro’s key performance outcomes (including System Reliability). This will
further deepen the utility’s “least cost” optimization approach by increasing the consistency and
objectivity of these evaluations at the project level.
Outside of this programmatic approach to investment planning, the utility also endeavors to offer
customers value-for-money by exploring new technologies adopted by the industry, which may be
more cost-effective than the current status quo. Toronto Hydro’s Product Change Committee
reviews and conducts pilot projects to assess the feasibility of new technologies and products.
Typically, after a detailed pilot phase, the technology or product is evaluated for its cost-
effectiveness in contributing to the utility’s objectives, including the improvement of system
reliability. For example, following a successful evaluation of mid-line reclosers through multiple
pilot projects, the utility is now proceeding to deploy this innovative and cost-effective technology
system-wide (Exhibit 2B, Section E7.1). The additional reliability benefits, such as reducing
interruption frequency and duration for customers, supplement the remotely operated SCADA
switches that Toronto Hydro has used for decades.

Toronto Hydro views its reliability performance as acceptable, both in comparison to historical data
and in competitiveness among its peers. The utility continuously assesses reliability performance
and trends relative to historical data, using measures reported on the EDS, as well as internally
tracked measures. Toronto Hydro also completed a Reliability Benchmark study as part of
developing this rate application, as detailed in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 3, Appendix A. In
addition to tracking reliability measures, the utility investigates outages that significantly impact its
customers on a weekly basis. In addition to interruptions originating from the distribution system,
Toronto Hydro works in close partnership with Hydro One to ensure Loss of Supply events are
investigated thoroughly and mitigated through appropriate action.
Toronto Hydro recognizes that on-going investments are required to maintain current levels of
reliability performance and developed a plan that largely maintains system reliability over the next
rate period while investing in modernization efforts capable of providing reliability benefits over
the longer term to manage the impacts of electrification and other pressures and complexities.
Please refer to the response to part (a) above, which describes the utility’s programmatic,
outcomes-focused, least-cost approach to investment planning.

question:
From Table 1: 2025-2029 Performance Objectives Toronto Hydro states: “Improve system reliability
through enhanced fault management, leveraging automation and advanced metering through AMI
2.0”

a) On its face, this objective conflicts with the “Maintain Reliability” objective cited in the
Sustainment and Stewardship investment priority. Please explain how Toronto Hydro
harmonizes these conflicting objectives when assembling its investment portfolio?
response:
Toronto Hydro’s objectives for the “Sustainment and Stewardship” and “Modernization” categories
address different (overlapping) time horizons and are fundamentally compatible. For Sustainment
and Stewardship, the reliability objective for the lagging indicators of SAIDI/SAIFI (and in particular,
SAIFI due to Defective Equipment) is to maintain current levels of performance over the 2025-2029
period by moving forward with a paced investment strategy that manages the deterioration of
assets and maintains (but does not improve) overall population health through the rate period. For
Modernization, Toronto Hydro is looking beyond 2029 in preparation for increasing pressures from
electrification, DERs, and climate change (as discussed in Exhibit 2B, Section E2, pages 18-20). It is
over this longer time horizon that Toronto Hydro is aiming to improve system reliability (and
resiliency) through modernization. While these investments have a long-term focus, Toronto Hydro
recognizes that there will be benefits to reliability as these technologies are gradually deployed
throughout this rate period. These benefits are reflected in the SAIDI and SAIFI projections shown
in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1, Figures 1 and 2.

question:
From Table 1: 2025-2029 Performance Objectives Toronto Hydro states: “Connect customers
efficiently and with consideration for an increase in connections volumes due to electrification”
“Expand stations capacity to alleviate future load constraints, with consideration for increased EV
uptake, decarbonization drivers, and other growth factors (digitization and redevelopment)”

a) What analysis does Toronto Hydro undertake to evaluate the risk of temporarily or
permanently stranding capital investments should the anticipated connection volume
trends fail to materialize over the planning period, to align with the principle of “least
regrets” investments?
response:
Toronto Hydro relies on its Capacity Planning process to adequately size capacity expansion efforts
to deliver reliable service and timely connections to its customers, resulting in its “least regrets”
planning approach. In order to identify and minimize the risk of temporarily or permanently
stranding capital investments, Toronto Hydro relies on a robust System Peak Demand Forecast
methodology, that is updated annually, that integrates a number of drivers of growth. Toronto
Hydro enhanced this methodology to consider additional factors ahead of preparing the 10-year
forecast that informed the 2025-2029 rate period. In addition, to support its decision-making
Toronto Hydro leveraged a long-term, multi-scenario growth modelling tool known as the Future
Energy Scenarios (“FES”) model to understand the range of possible scenarios under varying policy,
technology, and consumer behaviour. Please refer to Exhibit 2B, Section D4 for more details on
Toronto Hydro’s capacity planning process.
Integral to the planning process enhancements has been the integration of the use of Local
Demand Response in the assessment of alternatives to traditional wires investments. This provides
Toronto Hydro with the ability to monitor the realization of needs before committing to longer
term investments in growing system capacity.
These approaches, along with coordinated planning with key stakeholders such as Hydro One (the
transmitter) and the Independent Electricity System Operator, allow Toronto Hydro to assess
capacity needs for its system carefully and minimize the risk of stranding capital investments.

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “The utility developed initial capital program expenditure proposals with the
aim of fulfilling strategic objectives in the focus areas of Growth, Sustainment, Modernization and
General Plant. From this starting point, an iterative process generated multiple versions of the
capital expenditure plan, eventually producing a draft plan that formed the basis of Phase 2 of
Customer Engagement. The differences between the initial version of the plan - which on an
aggregate basis was higher than the $4,000 upper limit on capital expenditures.”

a) How was the upper limit capital expenditure envelope size of $4 billion determined?
b) Does the resulting capital expenditure plan satisfy Toronto Hydro’s acceptable risk
exposure assessment?
i)
If yes, does this indicate that the initial capital expenditure plan was larger than
necessary?
ii) If no, is Toronto Hydro’s position that the proposed capital expenditure plan is
imprudent?
c) Given that the capital expenditure constraints that were imposed appear to have been
generated top-down, rather than using Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management processes,
please explain how Toronto Hydro validated that the resulting solution is optimal as per
Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management or Risk Management processes.
d) Please provide documentation demonstrating that capital expenditure levels lower than
the $4 billion upper limit did not satisfy Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management and Risk
Management processes.
response:
Please refer to the response to interrogatory 2B-SEC-33.

Yes. Through an iterative and integrated planning process, the initial capital expenditure plan was
adjusted/constrained to arrive at a balance between price and outcomes that Toronto Hydro’s
deemed to be acceptable. Achieving this balance necessarily meant taking on some additional risk
and/or reducing the pace of progress in certain areas of the plan, as explained in the evidence at
Exhibit 2B, Section E2 page 7. For example, the Downtown Contingency segment of System
Enhancements was substantially reduced by focusing on creating station switchgear ties between
Copeland Station and Esplanade Station to manage (rather than alleviate) contingency concerns
within the downtown system.

The capital expenditure plan is the output of an iterative planning process that centered around
Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management system. Leveraging the analytical tools and risk-based decision-
making frameworks contained with the Asset Management system and processes described in
Exhibit 2B, Section D1, along with other relevant inputs and information, Toronto Hydro was able to
adjust/constrain the initial plan to arrive at a balance between price and outcomes deemed to be
acceptable from a risk perspective. For example, the Cable Chamber Renewal segment within the
Underground Renewal - Downtown program was reduced by approximately $25 million by scaling
back the number of poor condition assets to be addressed in the next rate period. The risk associated
with this reduction was deemed to be acceptable by targeting asset locations that have the highest
failure consequences.

The System Renewal evidence in Exhibit 2B, Section E6 demonstrates that the capital expenditures
proposed are aligned with Toronto Hydro’s Asset Management and Risk Management processes.
Please refer to the Appendix A1 at page 10 filed in response to 1A-CCC-01 for a high-level summary
analysis of capital expenditure levels lower than the $4 billion upper limit.

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “Toronto Hydro is expanding inspection and maintenance activities in key
areas through the Preventative and Predictive maintenance programs, resulting in an 11 percent
increase between 2024 and 2025, followed by a moderate 1 percent average annual increase from
2026-2029.”

a) Toronto Hydro is significantly increasing spending in at least three areas that directly affect
system reliability, i) System Renewal spending by 35%, ii) System Service - System
Enhancement program spending by 473%, and iii) Preventative and Predictive maintenance
program spending by 11% followed by 1% compounding, in addition to significant amount
of other program spending increases that will either directly or indirectly improve system
reliability. Please reconcile these parallel spending increases with Toronto Hydro’s strategy
of maintaining reliability in response to indicated customer preferences.
response:
Toronto Hydro is investing the minimum necessary to manage asset risk and achieve the goal of
maintaining system reliability as measured by SAIFI Defective Equipment. The increase in System
Renewal expenditures is driven by a number of factors, including inflation. Please see Toronto
Hydro’s response to 2B-Staff-169 for a discussion regarding the drivers of the increase in capital
expenditures within the System Renewal category.
Please see Toronto Hydro’s response to 2B-Staff-175 for more details on how investments in the
“Modernization” category reconcile with Toronto Hydro’s objective to maintain reliability over
2025-2029.
The increases in Toronto Hydro’s Preventative and Predictive maintenance programs support the
utility’s objective to maintain reliability and are largely complementary to System Renewal
investments, and meet outcomes in other areas such as safety and environment in addition to
reliability outcomes. As such, the increase in the preventative and predictive maintenance programs
are not solely driven by reliability considerations. Below is a list of other factors that drive these
increases:
•
As discussed in Exhibit 2B, Section D3.1.1, a large majority of preventative programs are
cyclical in nature in alignment with regulatory requirements.
•
Inspections serve as the primary input into Toronto Hydro’s Asset Condition Assessment
(“ACA”) methodology, which is a key input for decision-making within System Renewal
programs. For example, Toronto Hydro intends to increase the maintenance schedule for
wood poles from 10 years to 8 years in order to improve the collection of condition
information for this asset class.
•
Increases in asset populations naturally drive increases in inspection and maintenance
expenditures.
•
The introduction of new technologies and increased penetration of DERs on the system
also drive incremental inspection and maintenance requirements.
•
Inflationary pressures are expected to drive costs, especially within the Stations
maintenance programs.

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “The increase in the Corrective Maintenance Program is driven by
the need to address a growing backlog of P3 deficiencies within the system.”

a) Is the planned 35% increase in Renewal spending expected to help address the backlog of
P3 deficiencies within the system?
i.
If yes, does this mean that the Corrective Maintenance Program will be reduced in
future test periods? Please explain.
ii.
If no, are P3 deficiencies not correlated with asset condition, or is the planned
Renewal spending not being directed to assets with P3 deficiencies that require
urgent attention? Please explain.
response:
Toronto Hydro does not expect the planned 35 percent increase in Renewal spending to materially
help address the backlog of P3 deficiencies for the following reasons:
•
The Renewal spending increase is driven by a number of factors, which are discussed in
Toronto Hydro’s response to interrogatory 2B-Staff-169 (a), but as noted in Exhibit 2B,
Section E2.1.1 at page 3, one of the key objectives is to manage asset risk by maintaining
overall health demographics of the asset population.
•
As discussed in Exhibit 2B, Section D3.1.1.3, even if the increased spending did lead to
materially improved health demographics, this would not necessarily lead to a
corresponding reduction in the volume of deficiencies requiring corrective maintenance as
younger and healthier assets with defects may be more suited to being repaired than
replaced.
•
Planned renewal investments may support in addressing some of the backlog of P3
deficiencies where they happen to intersect with assets or areas targeted for capital
intervention. However, based on recent historical data, on average there has been less
than 1 percent of P3 work cancelled due to overlap with planned projects and therefore
any impact is expected to be very limited.
ii. Toronto Hydro respectfully rejects the premise of the last part of the question. P3 deficiencies
can be, but are not necessarily, related to asset condition. The P3 backlog includes
deficiencies, such as tripping hazards1 and nomenclature updates, which are unrelated to the
condition of an asset. In addition, as noted above, renewal expenditures are targeted to
maintaining, and not improving, overall asset health demographics and as such would not be
expected to impact overall P3 deficiency volumes even if there was a close correlation.
With respect to the idea of the utility’s planned renewal not being directed to P3 deficiencies
that require urgent attention, Toronto Hydro agrees that planned renewal is not generally
being directed to P3 deficiencies and notes that it should not be, but disagrees that P3
deficiencies require urgent attention. By definition, P3 deficiencies are the lowest priority, and
therefore the least urgent deficiencies requiring attention.2 Where asset replacement (i.e.
capital work) is required to address the deficiencies, these are carried out through the Reactive
capital segment (Exhibit 2B, Section E6.7); otherwise, deficiencies are addressed through the
Corrective Maintenance program (Tab 2, Schedule 4). Therefore, Toronto Hydro notes that the
P3 backlog referenced consists of the lowest priority deficiencies, specifically to be addressed
through Corrective Maintenance. Corrective maintenance allows Toronto Hydro to address
repairable issues in the short term in order to maximize performance of an asset, which in turn
may defer the need to replace the asset.
1 For example tripping hazards unrelated to underlying civil asset deterioration such as unlevel ground
around Toronto Hydro assets.
2 While less urgent than P1 or P2 deficiencies, Toronto Hydro still needs to P3 deficiencies before they
worsen and lead to bigger issues, unlike P4 deficiencies, which are the lowest priority identified and which
require monitoring only.

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “With the proliferation of DER in Toronto in recent years, several feeder
circuits have already surpassed the generation to minimum load ratio of one-third. A total of
eleven distribution feeders have ratios ranging from 0.30 to 11.51 (refer to Table 6: Existing
Feeders with Generation to Load Ratio Greater Than One-Third below). These feeders currently
present an increased risk of unintentional islanding conditions to the distribution system.”

a) Does Toronto Hydro calculate the expected output of DERs at the time of minimum feeder
loading, or does Toronto Hydro use nameplate DER rating in its feeder analysis?
i.
If yes, does this mean that solar DERs, which can be expected to have zero
production at the time of minimum feeder loading (typically during nighttime light
load hours), are being overcounted in Toronto Hydro’s analysis? Please explain.
response:
Toronto Hydro currently uses the nameplate DER system rating in its feeder analysis irrespective of
time day intervals. The utility does not have control over when exactly the minimum feeder load
condition will occur, and therefore to mitigate risk to the system, Toronto Hydro seeks to comply
with the IEEE 1547 requirement for anti-islanding which states that aggregate DER capacity is to be
less than one-third of the minimum load. This is further detailed in Exhibit 2B, Section E5.5, page
10. Modification of this approach will be considered as more tools are developed to interface with
DER’s in a dynamic operational environment.

question:
a) Rear Lot conversion spending is forecast to increase by $58.7M (95%) relative to historical.
Considering that Toronto Hydro has been implementing this conversion program for some
time, and presumably the most problematic segments have been addressed first, what has
changed to drive this sudden doubling in planned program spending?
b) Do any of the feeders being improved via the Rear Lot program also appear on the worst
performing feeder list?
i.
If yes, does Toronto Hydro intend to offset the proposed increase in Rear Lot
spending by commensurately reducing spending on the Worst Performing Feeders
program?
c) Does Toronto Hydro anticipate that completion of the Rear Lot program will improve or
maintain its overall reliability performance?
d) Please provide the total contribution of Rear Lot outages to Toronto Hydro’s SAIDI and
SAIFI results for 2012-2022.
response:
The Rear Lot segment for the 2025-2029 period has increased by 6 percent compared to what
Toronto Hydro proposed in the 2020 CIR application for 2020-2024. This increase is driven by
inflationary pressures and not pacing, which is consistent with the 2020-2024 proposal. The
reduced pace relative to what was proposed for 2020-2024 (in accordance with the OEB’s decision)
has contributed to increased need for investment in rear lot areas, which continue to deteriorate
with new areas starting to experience worsening reliability. Therefore, if anything, the proposed
pace of investment over 2025-2029 is conservative and Toronto Hydro expects that, beyond 2029,
it will need to maintain this pace or even increase it as these areas continue to age and deteriorate
(see Figure 3 in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.1 at page 6).

The Rear Lot program feeders don’t overlap with feeders addressed by the Worst Performing
Feeder program. While the Worst Performing Feeder target those with higher frequency of
outages, the rear lot feeders are targeted based on the duration of the outages and the challenges
they pose due to legacy equipment and safety concerns.

Rear Lot conversion is expected to eliminate tree contacts and reduce outage duration on those
areas converted and therefore, improve reliability for customers in those areas, who tend to
experience below-average reliability. The completion of the Rear Lot Conversion program will take
decades and if viewed in the long-term (i.e., by comparing reliability in the 2020s versus 2050s post
completion), may see some improvements that could be attributed to the conversions (and which
may be offset by other factors). However, for 2025-2029, Toronto Hydro expects rear lot
conversions to contribute to maintaining its overall reliability performance.

Rear Lot outages contributed to 4 percent to Toronto Hydro’s SAIDI performance and 2 percent to
SAIFI performance over 2012-2022.

question:
Toronto Hydro states “As of 2022, there are 286 circuit-kilometers of direct-buried cable in dirt.”

a) What would be the expected impact on Toronto Hydro’s SAIDI and SAIFI if the underground
cable replacement program focused upon replacing the cables that are buried in dirt for
the period 2025-29? In your answer, discuss Toronto Hydro’s claim that XLPE cables
installed in PVC ducts have expected service lives double those of XLPE cables directly
buried in dirt.
b) What is the annual expected failure rate per km for XLPE cables that are buried in dirt and
for cables installed in PVC ducts?
c) What is causing the PVC ducts to become clogged with dirt?
d) What mitigation alternatives are there to clear the dirt from these PVC ducts other than
replacing the cables?
i.
For the mitigation alternatives please provide comparative unit costing relative to cable
replacement.
e) Please explain the scope of Toronto Hydro’s plans to “install new TRXLPE cable in concrete-
encased ducts instead of burying cable directly into the soil or in PVC duct” throughout the
horseshoe area. For example, is the concrete-encasement for road crossings only, or road
crossings and industrial locations.
i.
If the ducts are to be concrete encased in residential neighbourhoods, please provide
the business case for the incremental costs and any examples of other jurisdictions that
have similar construction standards.
response:
In a hypothetical scenario where Toronto Hydro replaces only the remaining population of direct-
buried cable in dirt (286 circuit-kilometers) during the 2025-2029 rate period, it anticipates that the
cumulative impact on SAIFI and SAIDI for Defective Equipment interruptions would deteriorate by
6% and 5%, respectively, by the end of 2029, compared to Toronto Hydro’s proposed 2025-2029
investment plan. This scenario does not replace any cables in PVC conduit or concrete-encased ducts.
Due to the contiguous and integrated nature of Horseshoe distribution assets, this scenario is
unrealistic. Toronto Hydro will inevitably need to replace some minimum amount of cable in PVC
conduit and concrete-encased ducts as part of larger rebuild projects and in conjunction with other
asset types. Furthermore, Toronto Hydro has included cables in PVC conduit and concrete-encased
duct for replacement because these asset populations include aging cables at risk of failure, which
should be addressed as part of a balanced underground renewal program.
Direct-buried cable in dirt has a useful life of 20 years, whereas cable in PVC conduit has a useful life
of 50 years. The longer useful life for PVC Conduit is due to its enhanced protection against
environmental conditions and mechanical stresses. For information on how Toronto Hydro
determines its asset useful lives, please see response to 2B-Staff-131, part (a). Regardless of the
different useful life values, failures can and do occur for cables in PVC conduit due to aging and a
multitude of other factors, including insulation breakdown, moisture ingress, and overload.

Toronto Hydro estimates the historical failure rate (system interruptions per km) for direct-buried
cable in dirt to be 0.11 and for cable in PVC conduit to be 0.12.

PVC ducts can become clogged with dirt due to the following reasons:
•
Some vintages of PVC ducts that have been installed in the past are of inferior quality and
are prone to breakage
•
Improper installation or ducts not being connected in a closed loop
•
Unused ducts that are not properly sealed can experience dirt ingress; the dirt can be
pushed further into the duct by ground water or local flooding events

Toronto Hydro does not clear dirt from PVC ducts while the cable is in place. If the cable is
functioning as required and there is a problem with the duct (clogged or damaged), Toronto Hydro
will leave the cable until it needs to be replaced due to failure or a change in service, or until
planned replacement can be carried out at the appropriate time. At the time a cable is being
replaced, non-intrusive (plastic) mandrels are used to clear PVC ducts, provided there is space to fit
a mandrel. Should the mandrel prove insufficient, alternative solutions, including installing new
ducts or cleaning them out via power wash are considered.
Due to a drafting error, the explanation provided in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.2 incorrectly suggests
that the issue of PVC ducts filling with dirt is a new or emerging issue driving incremental
replacement. Toronto Hydro would like to clarify that this is not the case. The existing underground
cable population in the Horseshoe consists of three predominant types, two of which (direct-buried
cable in dirt and cable in PVC conduit) are legacy, obsolete standards. Cables in all three
construction types (including concrete-encased ducts) experience failures and are addressed in
different proportions by the planned investments in the Underground System Renewal –
Horseshoe program. The utility expects that as the direct-buried cable population reduces through
replacement, and cables in PVC conduit continue to age, cables in PVC conduit will become an
increasing focus of the program.

Toronto Hydro’s long-established policy for rebuilding underground areas is to install underground
cable in concrete-encased duct up to the lot-line. The issue of concrete-encasement and
alternatives was adjudicated by the Ontario Energy Board in Toronto Hydro’s 2012-2014
Incremental Capital Module application (EB-2012-0064). As written in the Board’s Partial Decision
and Order (April 2, 2013):
“While no party challenged THESL’s assessment of the need to replace this cable, Energy
Probe cross-examined THESL’s witnesses extensively on possible alternatives to THESL’s
plan to replace this cable with concrete encased ducts. THESL’s uncontradicted evidence
was that the suggested alternatives were unsuitable in the situations encountered by
THESL and that its approach was the most cost effective over the long term. Energy Probe
argued that a reduction of $10 million should be made to reflect the fact that THESL’s
proposal for concrete encased duct banks is not justified from a reliability standpoint and
that alternatives such as direct boring and flexible conduit or direct burying are acceptable
alternatives and much more cost effective. THESL argued that Energy Probe’s position
should be rejected by the Board since initial installation cost is not the only cost and
THESL’s evidence had presented substantial information on the repair cost advantages for
cable in concrete encased ducts which had been ignored by Energy Probe. THESL also
stated that its evidence had clearly explained that concrete encased ducts offer the longest
life and greatest reliability and facilitate future repair and replacement.” (pg. 22-23)
“The Board accepts THESL’s evidence that the most effective way to replace the direct
buried cable is with concrete encased ducts, and that the project is prudent and
nondiscretionary. There was no credible evidence to support the alternatives or reductions
sought by the intervenors. Having found that the work is required and prudent, any
reduction to the program is arbitrary and not supported by any evidence.” (pg. 24)

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “As of 2022, 26 percent of underground transformers in the Horseshoe area
(i.e. 6,727 units) were at or beyond useful life (i.e. 30 years for padmount, submersible, and vault
transformers).”

a) Please explain how Toronto Hydro determined that the useful life for padmount,
submersible and vault transformers should be set at 30 years, given that in 2022 6,727 of
these transformers had been in service for more than 30 years, and in some cases
significantly more than 30 years. In your response consider the information shown in Table
5 indicating that just 79 units out of the entire fleet of 25,209 units were assessed as being
in HI5 - End of Serviceable Life condition in 2022, despite 6,727 of the units age-categorized
as being beyond useful life.
response:
The useful life of 30 years was adopted based on a review of the Depreciation Study completed by
Concentric Inc., filed in Exhibit 2A, Tab 2, Schedule 1, Appendix D. Please see response to 2B-Staff-
131, part (a), for a discussion regarding Toronto Hydro’s useful lives and the extent to which they
play a role in investment planning decisions. Please also see the response to 2B-SEC-44 for a
comprehensive discussion regarding expected changes in asset demographics over the 2025-2029
period with investment.
Regarding Table 5 in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.2, the relatively small number of transformers in the
worst condition band (HI5) as of 2022 is a positive indication as to the effectiveness of Toronto
Hydro’s prioritization of the worst condition assets in investment planning. The fact that there were
approximately 640 transformers in HI4 and HI5 condition in 2022 while over 6,500 units were
operating beyond useful life underscores the benefits of having a robust condition model, which
allows Toronto Hydro to focus more narrowly on replacing assets and rebuilding areas of the
system that are most in need of investment.

question:
a) Toronto Hydro plans to increase Horseshoe Underground System Renewal spending by
$115.9M (32%) in 2025-2029 relative to 2020-2024. Please explain the spending increase in
the context of Toronto Hydro’s stated corporate goal of maintaining reliability performance
and the improving reliability performance outcomes achieved for these assets at historical
expenditure levels.
response:
Exhibit 2B, Section E6.2 provides detailed analysis on the drivers and key assumptions behind the
level of proposed expenditures in the Underground System Renewal – Horseshoe program.
Toronto Hydro has proposed the minimum expenditures necessary to maintain reliability on this
part of the system during the 2025-2029 period. The proposed investments are reflected in the
SAIDI and SAIFI forecasts presented in Exhibit 1B, Tab 3, Schedule 1.
The reliability improvement trend that persisted between 2015-2019 was the result of significant
capital investment in the replacement of direct-buried cable and associated assets beginning in the
previous “ICM” period (circa. 2013), including an investment level of $115.5 million achieved in the
year 2015. The pace of investment in this program dropped to around $70 million per year in 2018
and 2019. While the link between investments in one year and reliability performance in the next is
clouded by the unpredictability of asset failure rates, Toronto Hydro notes that the previously
positive reliability trend became a negative trend beginning in 2020. As further discussed in Section
E6.2: “Through prioritized neighbourhood rebuild projects focused on replacement of high-risk
direct-buried cross-linked polyethylene (“XLPE”) cables, Toronto Hydro previously had success
reducing the number of customer interruptions due to cable failure, from over 200,000 per year in
2013 to approximately 105,000 in 2019. However, more recently Toronto Hydro shifted focus away
from rebuild projects addressing direct-buried cables in order to address the urgent environmental
risk associated with PCBs. As a result, customer interruptions (and other reliability indicators) have
started trending back up, reaching 199,000 in 2022.”

Hydro has planned for an achievable pace of 2,800 cable chamber lids over the 2025-2029 period,

Toronto Hydro is not aware of any injuries to workers or members of the public since 2020 due to

question:
Figure 1 indicates that less than a quarter of overhead system outages are caused by defective
equipment, yet Toronto Hydro is accelerating its overhead system renewal expenditures by
$139.5M (64%).

a) Please explain why Toronto Hydro is increasing spending by 64% above historical levels to
address a situation that is only responsible for 24% of historic overhead system outages.
b) Please discuss what Toronto Hydro is doing to address the other 75% of outages and
relevant costs.
response:
The increase in this program does not represent an “acceleration” of investments.
The proposed Overhead System Renewal budget for the 2025-2029 period is higher than the 2020-
2024 expenditures due primarily to the following reasons:
•
the addition of the Overhead Infrastructure Resiliency segment ($85.9 million), which is a
reintroduction and expansion of the work done through the Overhead Infrastructure
Relocation program in Toronto Hydro’s 2015-2019 Distribution System Plan;
•
the deferral of work in the Overhead System Renewal segment from the 2020-2024 period
into the 2025-2029 period, which was done to manage pressures across the broader capital
expenditure plan; and
•
inflationary increases.
Note that the proposed expenditure for the Overhead System Renewal segment (i.e. excluding the
Overhead Infrastructure Resiliency segment) for the 2025-2029 period is $272.8 million. This is
aligned with the original plan of $265.7 million in the 2020-2024 DSP (and would in fact represent a
reduction in spending after accounting for inflation).

While the Overhead System Renewal program is aimed at reducing the failure risk of overhead
equipment, these investments may contribute to other reliability improvements, such as:
•
A reduction of tree-contact outages by replacing bare conductors with tree-proof
conductors or relocating existing pole lines away from high vegetation areas,
•
A reduction of foreign interference outages by relocating poles lines in high traffic areas,
•
A reduction of unknown outages caused by tree contacts, animal contacts and incorrect
fuse protection settings by replacing existing overhead assets with new assets that meet
current standards.
Toronto Hydro also manages overhead reliability performance through the Area Conversions
(Section E6.1), Reactive and Corrective Capital (Section E6.7), System Enhancements (Section E7.1),
Preventative and Predictive Maintenance (Exhibit 4, Tab 2, Schedule 1) and Corrective
Maintenance (Exhibit 4, Tab 2, Schedule 4) programs.

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “Figure 15 illustrates that, despite ongoing renewal, approximately 287 poles
on average had to be replaced reactively per year between 2019 and 2022.”

a) What are the primary failure modes of wood poles that require reactive replacement, and
what are the most common triggering events?
b) On average, how many poles per year does Toronto Hydro replace (or retire) under all of its
capital and operating programs and projects; for example, road moves and widenings,
reactive capital (storms, vehicle accidents, treefalls), Back Lot program, Box Frame
program, voltage upgrades, underground conversions, and overhead system renewal?
c) What is the ratio of poles replaced under the overhead renewal program to the poles
replaced or retired under all other programs and projects?
d) Does Toronto Hydro consider all the pole replacements or retirements it is doing under
these other programs or projects when evaluating the need to replace poles under the
overhead system renewal program?
response:
Primary failure modes of wood poles are explained in Exhibit 4, Tab 2, Schedule 1 at pages 13-14
and Exhibit 2B, Section D2.2.1.2: Overhead Assets Failure Characteristics.
In summary, rot and decay are the most common and primary reasons for condemning a pole for
replacement as they can weaken the mechanical strength and structure of the pole, which is the
primary indicator of its health and remaining life. Ground rot at the base of the pole in particular is
the worst location for rot to be in as the base is the most vulnerable to environmental degradation.
Signs of mechanical damage such as holes or cracks and insect infestation, which can compromise
the structure are another trigger for replacement.

On average, Toronto Hydro replaces approximately 4,100 poles per year under of all its programs.

The average ratio of poles replaced under the overhead renewal program to the poles replaced or
retired under all other programs is approximately 35 percent. This number increases to 45 percent
if the poles replaced under the externally driven programs are excluded, which is another
significant contributor of pole replacements but is not driven by failure risk.

Yes, Toronto Hydro considers pole replacements under other programs when evaluating need
under the Overhead System Renewal program. Please refer to 2B-SEC-44 for a discussion regarding
expectations for wood pole replacements and demographic changes in the 2025-2029 period.

question:
Over the planning period Toronto Hydro plans to replace 8,337 poles over 4 years which yields an
average annual replacement rate of 2,084 poles per year. The condition assessment tables indicate
that the number of wood poles in Hi4 and Hi5 will increase by 9,459 in 2022 and 32,158 in 2029. If
Toronto Hydro was to maintain Hi4 and Hi5 at 2022 levels 22,699 poles would need to replaced
between 2022 and 2029, yielding an annual replace rate of 3,242 poles per year.

a) Toronto Hydro owns approximately 183,620 poles and approximately 107,000 wood poles
were evaluated for asset condition between 2018-2022. Please explain why approximately
76,620 poles were not evaluated for condition assessment.
b) Comparing the planned annual average replacement for wood poles of 2,084 per year to a
condition replacement rate of 3,242, a shortfall of 1,158 assets appears to exist. Please
explain how Toronto Hydro is achieving asset demographics, for example are there Hi4 and
Hi5 pole replacements occurring in other spending categories that close the observed
shortfall.
i.
Do the wood pole health indices for 2029 overstate the projected decay in wood
pole asset condition, given that Toronto Hydro’s consultant has indicated a
potential miscalculation of wood pole useful life.
response:
The total count of 183,620 poles mentioned in Exhibit 2B – Section A encompasses both
streetlighting and distribution poles within the system. Among these, distribution poles consist of
approximately 107,000 wood poles, 30,000 concrete poles, and 3,600 steel poles. Toronto Hydro's
Asset Condition Assessment methodology specifically focuses on distribution wood poles as they
are subject to a dedicated pole inspection program enabling the calculation of condition-based
Health Scores. The condition of the remaining poles (concrete and steel) has not been assessed due
to the lack of both a regular inspection program and an ACA methodology. Once inspections of
these poles commence, ACA methodology and condition-based Health Scores will be established.
Please refer to Exhibit 4, Tab 2, Schedule 1, Segment 5 for details regarding overhead line patrols
and pole inspections.

To clarify, the Overhead System Renewal program plans to replace 8,337 poles over five years,
which is an annual replacement of 1,667 poles per year from 2025-2029. If no investment or pole
replacement were done from 2022 till 2029, 32,158 poles are expected to reach HI4 and HI5
condition in 2029. Please see response to 2B-SEC-44 for a comprehensive overview of expected
changes in asset demographics over the 2025-2029 period with investment, including a discussion
regarding the utility’s decision to restrain the pace of pole replacements.
i.
In Toronto Hydro’s experience, wood poles have proven to be a uniquely challenging asset
to track and model from an ACA perspective. This is due primarily to the fact that
inspections occur only once every 10 years, meaning that the model is in many cases
relying on data that is upwards of nine years old. This, in Toronto Hydro’s view, is the most
significant factor in the comparatively high rate of deterioration seen in the Future Health
Score model outputs (since the model is having to age the assets over a longer period of
time, amplifying its effects). As discussed in Ex.2B, Section D3, App A, Toronto Hydro’s
assessment of the wood pole ACA model since its implementation in 2017 has led to
reasonable adjustments that better align model outputs with observed reality. Toronto
Hydro aims to further mitigate this issue through its proposed reduction of inspection to an
8-year cycle and by introducing targeted wood pole inspections based on the asset
condition assessment (see 2B-PWU-10).
Regarding the Normal Expected Life for assets, please refer to 2B-Staff-146.

question:
Regarding Table11: Power Transformers Proposed for Replacement

a) Please confirm Dunsany MS Power Transformer 2408, Centennial MS Power Transformer
2412 are all scheduled for replacement solely due to age and not because of additional
concerns.
i.
If not confirmed, please explain why not.
b) Explain why Belfield MS Power Transformer 2504 is scheduled for replacement in 2029 at
an age of 60 years despite exhibiting no concerns other than age, even though it will still be
5 years younger than Toronto Hydro’s reduced maximum target age of 65 for Power
Transformers in 2029.
response:
Power transformers replacements are not prioritized solely based on age. As described in Exhibit
2B, Section E6.6.4.2, Table 42 at page 56, Toronto Hydro considers the impact of failure, such as
customer count, loading, degradation of oil, resiliency of operation, and voltage conversion plan in
addition to age when prioritizing the replacement these assets. On average, the average Municipal
Station (“MS”) supplies approximately 500 customers. However, Centennial MS and Dunsany MS
supply around 700 and 750 customers, respectively which represent 39 and 49 percent more than
the average number of customers. As such, they are assigned a higher priority for replacement.

Belfield Municipal Station consists of two Power Transformers (TR1 2503 and TR2 2504). As shown
in Table 42 in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.6.4.2 at page 56, the need to replace Belfield MS Power
Transformer 2504 is not solely based on age but due to the combination of age with the following:
•
TR1 2503 will be 69 years old at the time of the project and has a high-power factor;
•
A loading analysis of the area identified the need for only one power transformer,
therefore resulting in the removal of TR2 2504 and replacement of TR1 2503;
•
The primary supply to the MS also requires replacement due to the high risk of failure of
direct buried ingress; and
•
Belfield MS Switchgear is planned to be replaced in 2029. Coordination of the replacement
in conjunction with the aforementioned work is a cost-effective alternative.

$36.6M (130%).

a) What is the annual probability of failure of any of the existing electromechanical relays?
b) Are electromechanical relay failures trending up significantly?

significantly increased planned spending on relay replacements relative to the historical
period? Please discuss.

obsolete or poor condition breakers or switchgear?
response:
Protection relay systems have built in redundancies that allow back-up systems to operate in the
event of a single relay failure; and are inspected as part of a robust maintenance cycle. As such,
Toronto Hydro does not track individual relay failures and is unable to provide their probability of
failure or an indication whether electrotechnical relay failures are trending up

Confirmed. Toronto Hydro’s planned investments in relays over the 2025-2029 period are driven by
a combination of system observability, equipment obsolescence and improved fault location and
protection equipment coordination. Modernizing old electromechanical relays to digital relays have
other benefits for the system that reduces maintenance costs, improves reliability, and enhances
grid observability. For more detail, please refer to Control and Monitoring drivers at Exhibit 2B,
Section E6.6.3.3 and Grid Modernization Section D5.1.

As the monitoring and control work is carried out on a programmatic basis, Toronto Hydro cannot
readily identify which relays are specifically linked to obsolete and poor condition breakers and
switchgear outside of specific assets identified in project scopes and details.
To clarify, Toronto Hydro replaces electromechanical relays either through targeted renewal or as
part of a switchgear/breaker replacement.1 As described in response to part (c), the proposed
investments are driven by station modernization to enhance system and station observability and
improve fault location. The latter is done in conjunction with switchgear and breaker replacement.
Toronto Hydro notes that the 2025-2029 relay investments proposed in the Monitoring and Control
segment do not overlap with planned switchgear and breaker replacements.

Similarly, Toronto Hydro made a load true-up payment for the historic project, Cecil TS T3/T4
Upgrade which was executed in 2005. The payment was the result of differences in Toronto
Hydro’s 2021 System Peak Demand Forecast relative to Toronto Hydro’s 2015 System Peak
Demand Forecast, submitted for each respective true-up evaluation. This difference is attributed
to lack of load realization from customers relative to load requested over the 2013-2017 period,
and the impact of COVID-19 in the Cecil area. Additionally, as the in-service date for Copeland
Phase II had not been set at the time of the 2015 forecast, it did not reflect the impact of future
load transfers from Cecil to Copeland TS (post-Phase 2). These transfers were reflected in the 2021
forecast which formed the basis of the true-up.

question:
Figure 15: 2019-2029 Reactive Capital Work Requests Actuals and Forecast shows that the number
of work requests decreased from 2019 to 2021 and increased slightly in 2022. Toronto Hydro
predicts a steady level of work requests over the forecast period.

a) Please explain the trend of work requests in this budget category.
response:
As described in Exhibit 2B, Section E6.7, the work under the Reactive Capital segment is unplanned,
unpredictable and non-discretionary. Hence, the data from year to year can vary significantly since
the work is demand driven. The consistent decline in the number of work requests from 2019 to
2021 primarily stems from a reduction in the instances of oil leaks necessitating reactive
transformer replacements. As Toronto Hydro continues to substitute non-submersible/non-
stainless-steel transformers with stainless steel ones through its renewal programs, Toronto Hydro
anticipates this decline in failures to persist and stabilize. Conversely, the incidence of deficiencies
prompting reactive pole replacement requests has been increasing, attributed to the increasing
number of poles surpassing their useful life and experiencing deteriorating asset condition.

question:
a) Confirm that the System Enhancements program will reduce the consequence of individual
asset failures in many or most cases.
i.
If not confirmed, explain the purpose of the program, since it will not reduce the
probability of asset failures.
response:
Confirmed. Please refer to Exhibit 2B, Section E7.1, Page 5 for specific information on this topic.
Note that Toronto Hydro respectfully disagrees with the premise of part (i) of OEB Staff’s question.
The System Enhancements program contains a variety of field technology investments which will
deliver benefits beyond reducing consequences of failure. The proposed System Observability
segment of the program includes adding more sensors, relays and monitoring technology at
specific nodes across the distribution grid. Gradually, these technologies will help the utility
advance three core capabilities:
1. Enhanced Fault Location: Locating faults and other system disturbances faster and more
efficiently in order to improve reliability and operate the grid more cost-effectively.
2. Enhanced Decision-making and Grid Optimization: Providing greater insight into real-time
feeder and asset loading, condition, and other relevant operating characteristics. This
assists the utility in managing short- and long-term uncertainty as well as driving optimal
real-time operational decisions and longer-term investment planning decisions.
3. Enhanced Asset Diagnostics: Greater visibility into high-risk and previously hard-to-
monitor assets will improve asset diagnostics, mitigating the risk of asset failure and
impacts to personnel safety and environmental damage.
For more information on the multi-faceted benefits of Toronto Hydro’s System Enhancements
program, please refer to Exhibit 2B, Section E7, and the Intelligent Grid Section of Toronto Hydro’s
Grid Modernization Strategy (Exhibit 2B, Section D5.2.1).

question:
Toronto Hydro states: “The NWS strategy for the 2025-2029 period is focused on being flexible and
adaptable to help system planners respond to load growth while navigating the underlying
uncertainty that stems from changing demand patterns and increased reliance on electrification.
This strategy builds on Toronto Hydro’s experience utilizing DERs to reduce peak demand, helping
to defer grid expansions or, in most cases, avoid grid expansions should demand not materialize as
expected (e.g., lower than expected demand, fluctuating demand).”

a) Please quantify by technology type the alignment of energy production by the DERs
presently installed in Toronto Hydro’s service area with the summer and winter peak
demand hours on Toronto Hydro’s distribution system.
b) Given the response to the prior question, please describe the effectiveness of Toronto
Hydro’s existing DER portfolio in mitigating capacity constraints encountered by Toronto
Hydro during summer and winter peak demand periods.
response:
As outlined in Exhibit 2B Section E7.2, Toronto Hydro plans for and procures third-party capacity in
the form of dispatchable demand response to complement standard system planning approaches.
The utility is unable to provide the requested data as Toronto Hydro does not procure energy
(kWh) from DERs.

Toronto Hydro does not control third-party owned, non-dispatchable DERs and thus cannot rely
upon these assets to meet system needs (capacity needs or otherwise) on demand. Until a DER
owner enters into a binding agreement with Toronto Hydro (via LDR procurement) to provide a
specific service to the grid, Toronto Hydro will not consider this DER as a reliable system tool. As
part of its Local Demand Response program, Toronto Hydro procured 8 MW of dispatchable
demand response capacity between 2018-2020, 4 MW between 2022-2023, and 6 MW in 2024.
The non-wires solutions considered for the 2025-2029 rate period are described in Exhibit 2B
Section E7.2. Toronto Hydro’s use of NWSs is targeted and focuses on credible capital deferral
opportunities, and thus, the application of these solutions is limited to instances where such
deferral opportunities can be identified and measured. The use case identified at this time is
limited to bus-level load transfer deferral or avoidance. This can be achieved through the
procurement of dispatchable demand response from aggregators or customers. Toronto Hydro is
agnostic to the technology (type of DER) or approach (load curtailment) utilized by aggregators or
customers to deliver this demand response capacity. Participants are compensated based on
measured and verified performance, utilizing the methodology outlined in IESO’s Market Manual
12 – Issue 16.

question:
Toronto Hydro has proposed an expanded Energy Storage System as part of its Non-Wires
Solutions for 2025-2029 to assist in providing distribution-level grid support. Toronto Hydro
forecasts expenditures of $22.5 million over the 2025-2029 period to support the deployment of 9
projects with an aggregate capacity of 10.2 MW.
As part of the OEB’s Decision in EB-2018-0165 it provided direction that it expected Toronto Hydro
to respond to as part of any future application that seeks approval of Renewable Enabling
Investments and Energy Storage Systems, including evidence of the benefits to power quality,
reliability and capacity and an assessment of appropriate sharing of benefits for ESS projects as part
of future requests for funding for provincial rate protection.

a) Please discuss the pace of the BESS investment strategy. In particular, please provide more
detail regarding the process Toronto Hydro will undertake in determining when to proceed
with a BESS investment during the 2025-2029 term, including how Toronto Hydro plans to
overcome the challenges faced in the recent past (siting, supply chain, integration into the
existing system, low vendor interest).
b) Please discuss the status of the technical requirements currently in development to
support the standardized process of ESS design and procurement, including what Toronto
Hydro is using as the basis for the technical requirements.

proposal for the ESS plan.

developed, including the increase in planned expenditures in 2027 relative to other years.

broken out between that which is allocated to Toronto Hydro’s rate base (i.e. six percent or
$1.6 million) and that the remaining funding component through the provincial renewable
enabling improvement revenue stream.
f) Please provide an assessment of the appropriate sharing of benefits for the proposed BESS
projects between Toronto Hydro’s customers and broader electricity customers across
Ontario for those amounts requested to be recovered under the provincial renewable
enabling improvement funding component.

proposed to be behind-the-meter. If so, please discuss the nature of these projects and the
anticipated benefits.
h) Please discuss the analysis Toronto Hydro has undertaken to understand the pace of
battery technology evolution. As part of your response, please address how Toronto Hydro
will assess the long-term viability and performance of battery technologies installed. Please
also discuss the risk mitigation efforts to avoid investing in technologies that become
obsolete in a short period of time.
i)
The ESS strategy is being prioritized to reduce the minimum load to generation ratio for
specific feeder stations. Please discuss the process Toronto Hydro proposes to undertake
to assess the performance and reliability of planned BESS investments to ensure they meet
or exceed performance requirements.

Please discuss the consideration of life cycle environmental impacts of the planned BESS
investments, including the process to disposing of batteries after their useful life.

contribute to the resilience and security of Toronto Hydro’s system.

Response program, if at all.

Program developed in partnership with Toronto Metropolitan University.
response:
As described in Exhibit 2B Section 7.2.2, Toronto Hydro intends to install front-of-the-meter, utility-
